articles.title: The Potential Mismatch Between Japan and the US on China
articles.full_text:
Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, it is critical for Japan that the United States stays on the same page regarding the challenge from China.
Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae (right) shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump during their summit meeting in Tokyo, Japan, Oct. 28, 2025.
As the two most powerful countries in the world today, it is incredibly important that U.S. President Donald Trump will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24. But before that, Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae of Japan is hoping to gain a meeting with Trump during her own visit to the United States for the U.N. General Assembly. 
Both Trump and Takaichi are scheduled to address the General Debate in New York on September 22; as of September 17 “nothing has been decided” regarding a potential meeting, according to Takaichi. 
The China-U.S. summit will have broad implications across a variety of policy areas, and there is no shortage of things for Trump and Xi to talk about. But it will be especially important for Japan, given not just its alliance with the United States, but also its close geographic proximity to China. Takaichi thus hopes to meet with Trump and share Japan’s perspective on China, in order to make sure Japanese interests are considered by its foremost partner.
For Japan, China is a significant threat to its national security that needs to be managed with help from the United States. The security environment in the Indo-Pacific region is under pressure as China continues developing its military capabilities. According to Japan’s defense white paper released last month, “China has been intensifying its activities in the region surrounding Japan [and] extending beyond the so-called first island chain to the second island chain.” 
There are numerous examples of China putting pressure on Japan’s national security and ability to respond. It has upped its coast guard patrols around the island of Taiwan, creating a situation that could threaten Japanese security in the event of a contingency. Japan had to deploy fighters after Chinese and Russian planes were detected in airspace close to the Miyako Strait by Okinawa in June. And Beijing continues to send coast guard ships to patrol inside waters surrounding the disputed Senkaku Islands, claimed by China as the Diaoyu. 
While bilateral Sino-Japanese relations have always vacillated over historical disputes and national security concerns, the current state of the relationship is particularly frigid. It is critical for Japan that the United States – its principal ally and partner – stays on the same page regarding the challenge from China.
The U.S. shares some Japanese concerns about China. Like Tokyo, Washington remains concerned about Chinese assertiveness in the Indo-Pacific region. The U.S., Japan, and other states released a joint statement in August that was critical of China’s unannounced launch of submarine-based long-range ballistic missile. 
The U.S. continues to participate in multilateral military exercises focused on the Indo-Pacific, hosting the Rim of the Pacific exercises in Hawai’i in July, and participating in the May Balikatan exercises with the Philippines. Official references to the Indo-Pacific region are sparser than during the first Trump administration, but the U.S. continues to share its allies’ concerns about Chinese expansion in the region.
At the same time, there are differences between the U.S. and Japan. The conflict in Iran is arguably the Trump administration’s top priority. A report by the Department of Defense inspector general said the conflict was depleting U.S. supplies of important munitions. It has also necessitated the reassignment of the aircraft carrier USS George Washington to the Middle East from the Indo-Pacific region. 
Trump is not a Sinophile, and the U.S. continues to have interests at odds with China’s. But the long-term competition with China may not be as prominent in the mind of Trump, who is bogged down in Iran and related problems. He may be looking for China’s help to ameliorate the worst economic impacts of the war. For example, although the price of oil continues to rise because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, lowered Chinese demand is believed to have a moderating effect on the global oil market. 
To be sure, Washington can talk and chew gum at the same time. And it is not uncommon for allies to have different priorities in diplomacy. This means that the real question is to what extent the U.S. president will take into consideration the equities and viewpoints of allies like Japan. If there is a mismatch in those expectations, it will be critical for the alliance to deal with that friction. 
Two years into his second term, Trump seems to have established a cordial relationship with Takaichi. The broader alliance also remains a firm and important part of national security and diplomacy for both sides. But Japanese wariness about the upcoming Trump-Xi summit and its implications for the Indo-Pacific region are palpable. “With the decline in the U.S. military’s presence in Asia, aren’t China and North Korea taking advantage of this situation?” asked the Yomiuri Shimbun in a September editorial. 
It is difficult to see a major or irreversible rift developing between Washington and Tokyo. But a China-U.S. summit that leaves Japan’s interests out in the cold will be an unneeded challenge for the alliance at a critical time.
Takaichi undoubtedly knows that Trump is a free agent, and that he will do whatever he thinks will “make America great again.” When she meets with Trump ahead of his summit with Xi, her challenge will be to impress upon the U.S. president Japan’s perspective and why it is critical for the Japan-U.S. alliance to continue functioning at a close level. Although the alliance remains strong, a failure to coordinate could lead to friction in this relationship despite its importance to both Washington and Tokyo.

articles.title: Will Taiwan Fight? We Need Better Evidence.
articles.full_text:
Both those making pessimistic predictions and those confidently rejecting them often rely on thin evidence.
Simon Shuster’s recent article in The Atlantic, asking whether Taiwan might simply “give up” in the face of growing pressure from China, attracted considerable attention in Taiwan and among the broader community of China and Taiwan watchers. Some praised the piece for its candid analysis and for asking uncomfortable questions that are too often avoided in discussions about Taiwan’s security. Others were somewhat less impressed. 
The article quickly came under fire from Taiwanese and (mostly) Taiwan-based foreign analysts, who pointed to factual errors, questionable interpretations of domestic politics, and what they saw as a selective and misleading portrayal of Taiwanese society. Legislator Puma Shen, one of those interviewed for the article, issued a public statement accusing Shuster of taking his comments out of context. The Taipei Times devoted an editorial to rebutting the article, and even Taiwan’s National Security Council weighed in, with Secretary General Joseph Wu publicly rejecting its central premise.
Essentially, there are rather good reasons to take these criticisms seriously. Some concern basic facts and context, which are obviously important when making such a sweeping argument about Taiwan. That said, the reaction also exposed another problem. A significant part of the response has questioned what a foreign journalist who spent limited time in Taiwan and has no evident prior expertise on Taiwan or the region can really know about Taiwanese society. Critics pointed to a lack of understanding of Taiwanese politics, insufficient engagement with Taiwanese voices and opinion polls showing considerable willingness to defend Taiwan, and Taiwan’s own experience – from democratization and the Sunflower Movement to its remarkable response to COVID-19 – as evidence of a society capable of mobilizing when necessary.
As compelling as these arguments are, none of them give us a particularly convincing answer either.
Predicting what Taiwan and its people would actually do if China decided to use force is extraordinarily difficult. Both those making pessimistic predictions and those confidently rejecting them often seem to rely on evidence that tells us much less than we think.
Opinion polls are perhaps the clearest example. As argued previously in The Diplomat, they are useful for understanding attitudes, but telling a pollster that you would defend Taiwan is very different from making that decision when missiles are falling, casualties are mounting, electricity and communications are disrupted, and nobody knows whether outside help is coming. That does not make polls useless. Questions involving actual costs, such as longer military service, higher taxes, or greater personal obligations, can tell us more. But saying that you are willing to sacrifice something and actually sacrificing it are not the same thing.
Historical examples have only limited relevance. Taiwan’s democratization, the Sunflower Movement, and its response to COVID-19 have all been cited as evidence of a society capable of mobilizing when necessary. Comparisons can also be drawn with Finland’s resistance to the Soviet Union during the Winter War, Ukraine’s response to Russia’s invasion, or other societies that proved far more willing to resist than outsiders expected. These are indeed powerful examples. But what exactly do they tell us about how Taiwanese society would respond to a Chinese attack today?
Israel offers a useful example of why we should be careful in making predictions. Israeli society has repeatedly shown an extraordinary ability to mobilize against military threats. Following the October 7 attacks, more than 300,000 reservists were mobilized in a very short period, including Israelis who returned from abroad to report for duty. Nonetheless, during COVID-19, Israel struggled to sustain public compliance with government restrictions. Trust and willingness to follow regulations declined as the crisis continued. The same society generated two very different responses to calls for public action.
The type of threat, its perceived seriousness, public trust, political divisions, and personal costs can all shape how societies respond. Historical experience and comparisons can give us useful clues. But they cannot tell us what Taiwanese will do when confronted by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA).
So perhaps we need to look elsewhere. Instead of endlessly asking whether Taiwanese will fight or give up, we should look more closely at what Taiwanese society, its politicians, and its military are actually doing as the threat from China grows.
Taiwan has struggled with military recruitment and retention, personnel shortages, and a reserve force in which too few receive regular and meaningful training. Political polarization has repeatedly turned defense into another battlefield between the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and Kuomintang (KMT), most visibly in the continuing fights over defense spending. Institutional cooperation and coordination remain problematic, while deeply rooted institutional and military cultures can slow necessary reforms and adaptation. Taiwan also faces serious constraints in expanding its defense-industrial capacity quickly enough to meet its growing needs. All of these problems tell us something about how much Taiwanese citizens, politicians, and institutions are actually willing, and able, to change as the threat grows.
There are, however, signs that some things are moving in the right direction. After years of decline, military recruitment and retention have recently improved, although it is too early to know whether this represents a lasting reversal. Organizations such as Kuma Academy and Forward Alliance have attracted thousands of people who are willing to spend their own time on civil-defense training, and defense spending has increased substantially. Taiwan’s annual Han Kuang exercises have also become significantly more realistic and comprehensive, with this year’s iteration, Han Kuang 42, featuring longer and less scripted training, involving a broader range of military, government, and civilian actors, and placing much greater emphasis on whole-of-society defense.
This still isn’t definitive proof that Taiwanese will fight, nor does it negate the more troubling signs. But these are precisely the kinds of developments we should be watching. Are more people joining the military, and are they staying? Are reservists receiving more serious training? Are citizens willing to give their time to civil defense? Are Taiwanese willing to accept longer service, higher defense spending, or other personal costs? Are political leaders willing to put defense above partisan interests? Are government institutions actually cooperating and changing the way they operate? And is the military becoming more serious about preparing for the kind of war it may actually have to fight?
More importantly, we should follow these indicators over time. One bad year of military recruitment could be an aberration. A decline continuing for five or ten years as the threat grows tells us considerably more. The same is true of retention, reserve training, civil defense participation, defense spending, and military reform. 
We should also look at whether these indicators move in the same direction. If what Taiwanese tell pollsters corresponds with what citizens, politicians, and institutions are actually willing to do, we can have greater confidence in those attitudes. 
There is another complication. Talking about “Taiwan’s resilience” or “Taiwan’s will to fight” often treats Taiwan as a unitary actor when it clearly is not. The differences go well beyond the DPP-KMT divide. The military, government agencies, local authorities, civil society, businesses, and different parts of the public may have very different levels of preparedness, commitment, and willingness to bear costs. Reducing all of this to a single national characteristic risks obscuring more than it reveals.
To muddy the waters even more, resistance itself is not binary. “Will Taiwan fight?” or “Will Taiwan give up?” sounds straightforward, but what exactly are we imagining? A Chinese quarantine? A prolonged blockade? The seizure of an offshore island? Missile strikes? A full-scale invasion? Taiwanese might react very differently to each. 
Even after fighting begins, attitudes may change. A population initially determined to resist might think differently after weeks of casualties, shortages, and destruction. An attack could also have the opposite effect and produce much stronger determination. The military, political leaders, and broader public may respond differently, while much could depend on whether Taiwanese believe the United States or Japan will eventually intervene.
Ultimately, there is no fixed amount of “will to fight” sitting somewhere inside Taiwanese society waiting for the right journalist, pollster, or academic to discover it. That brings us back to Shuster. His article deserves criticism where its facts, evidence, and interpretations are wrong. But the same analytical standard should apply to those challenging his conclusions.
Nobody can confidently tell us exactly what Taiwan and its people will do if China uses force. We can, however, do a much better job of examining what they are doing now and how that changes over time. Indeed, it will not tell us for certain whether Taiwan will fight. But it does give us a much better place to start.

articles.title: The Space Security Landscape Is Deteriorating Rapidly
articles.full_text:
With the United States announcing that it has deployed “on-orbit space control weapons,” the space arms race now appears to be fully underway.
Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink delivers a keynote address during the 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference at the National Harbor, Md., Sept 14, 2026.
There is little doubt that great power competition is ramping up. Now, another front has opened, with the United States announcing that it has deployed a space weapon. China, and subsequently Russia, had been pushing the limits in space, testing advanced technologies with possible offensive uses in outer space, including cyber weapons, ground-based lasers, and artificial robotic arms that could be used for repairing satellites but also have obvious military and intelligence uses. Now the U.S. has responded by joining the developing arms race, which is likely to spur further competition. 
The space arms race now appears to be fully underway. 
The acknowledgement of U.S. space weapons was made by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink. He revealed that the U.S. Space Force has launched “space control weapons” into orbit. Delivering a keynote address at a recent Air and Space Forces Association (AFA) conference, Meink said that “the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.” 
Not surprisingly, he justified this step with reference to the threats from China and Russia, both of which “continue to demonstrate aggressive maneuvers and are developing – and demonstrating – space weapons of their own.” 
Meink is not the only U.S. official who has talked about these new space weapons. 
Addressing the “State of the Space Force” at the AFA conference, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess made an unequivocal claim that the U.S. Space Force “uses active space-based weaponry to support United States national defense.” He noted the “increasingly contested” space domain where adversaries have technologies that are meant to disrupt or destroy satellites in orbit. He also made a mention of hypersonic weapons that pose a threat to the United States and its allies and partners. 
While details are scanty and there has been no elaboration of the weapon systems that have been launched, this is clearly a recognition of and a response to what Russia and China have been doing in terms of their own space weapons. In fact, Meink dismissed ideas from journalists that the U.S. announcement of developing space control weapons could give permission to its adversaries pursuing space weapons. The race is already on.
Space is central to U.S. national security and war fighting efforts. The domain represents essential eyes and ears for military operations, which meant that the United States could not afford to ignore China and Russia’s threats and advancements. 
Threats to national assets in outer space have grown rapidly and are very diverse today. Just as the world seemed as if it was outgrowing fears about nuclear weapons, it was revealed that Russia was developing and potentially deploying nuclear anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons. If used, such weapons can result in the indiscriminate destruction of entire satellite orbits. These developments were revealed in February 2024 by U.S. intelligence officials. 
Kinetic anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons have also made a comeback since the first successful ASAT test by China in January 2007. China in effect broke an unwritten moratorium that had been in place since the 1980s. Since the Chinese ASAT test, others followed: the U.S. (2008), India (2019), and Russia (2021). The Russian ASAT test, using the A-235 / PL-19 Nudol kinetic interceptor missile system, resulted in the creation of “more than 1,500 pieces of trackable orbital debris” according to a statement from U.S. Space Command. The United States saw this as a direct effort to target it. 
Gen. James Dickinson, commander of the U.S. Space Command, stated that “Russia is developing and deploying capabilities to actively deny access to and use of space by the United States and its allies and partners.” He added that the test was a clear demonstration of the Russian pursuit of counterspace weapons that “undermine strategic stability and pose a threat to all nations.” 
Both the Chinese and Russian ASAT tests were also conducted at a higher altitude – 865 km and 480 km respectively – which would mean that the debris generated as a result would stay afloat in space orbits for decades because the atmosphere drag at that altitude is lower. 
In addition, there is an entire range of non-kinetic counterspace weapons that have been deployed in space, causing innumerable incidents of interference, disruptions, and destruction of space assets. Non-kinetic weapons include electromagnetic pulses, high-powered lasers, and high-powered microwaves, in addition to electronic and cyber options including jamming and spoofing as well as data interception and/or corruption and taking full control of data. All of these weapons have been employed and there have been growing incidents of space interference as far back as 2008. Attribution is difficult but many of these threats are thought to be sourced from Russia and China. 
Therefore, while the open U.S. claim about deployment of space weapons have made headlines everywhere, with many even suggesting that this will push Russia and China to develop such weapons, the reality is that Beijing and Moscow have been developing and employing these weapons, all while using the rhetoric of non-weaponization and peaceful use of space. Calls for non-weaponization and getting more countries to see the benefits of keeping space safe, secure, and sustainable are important, but this effort is increasingly being overtaken by a space arms race that now appears inevitable.

articles.title: China Is Building a Global Infrastructure for Its Cultural Industries
articles.full_text:
When a cultural industry expands overseas, that usually means exporting content. China is increasingly exporting the infrastructure behind entertainment products.
On September 4, Lingang New Area in Shanghai launched an AI+micro-drama overseas service station, with initial service points in Saudi Arabia, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland. The initiative is designed to help Chinese companies navigate overseas regulations, localize content, and connect production with distribution in foreign markets. The service station covers the full export chain including content development, production, translation, and distribution. Rather than simply helping companies sell finished dramas abroad, it brings several stages of the export process into one system. 
Online literature, games, and micro-dramas are increasingly described in China as the “New Three” of cultural exports. All three can be adapted, translated, and distributed through digital platforms, making the process of taking them overseas simpler.
In July, Guangxi Publishing & Media Group launched FLYTOTO, an AI-powered platform for short-drama co-creation. The platform connects Chinese production teams and creators with audiovisual institutions in Southeast Asia. FLYTOTO offers tools for script analysis, automated video production, and multilingual translation, alongside computing and distribution support. articles.title: BRICS Declaration: India’s Great U-turn on Iran
articles.full_text:
The declaration endorsed most of Iran’s main diplomatic concerns without speaking a single word against its drone and missile attacks on its neighboring Gulf states.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian being honored at a meeting with a group of Indian religious leaders, intellectuals, and businesspeople in New Delhi, India, on Sept. 11, 2026, the eve of the 18th BRICS Summit.
Before the BRICS summit in New Delhi, political analysts had warned that India would have to do a very difficult tightrope walk given the presence of China, Russia, and Iran. It was a foregone conclusion that they would use this platform for U.S. bashing. With India’s current tug-of-war with the Donald Trump administration, the honchos at South Block (India’s foreign ministry headquarters) used nuanced vocabulary and calibrated the final declaration in such a way that the United States was not named, but the declaration explicitly called for an end to unilateral economic sanctions, protectionist trade measures, and arbitrary tariffs.
The surprising outcome of the summit is this: what is being hailed as a triumph of strategic autonomy saw the dilution of India’s foreign policy since the advent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The BRICS summit was billed as the Modi show, but Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian stole that thunder if one looks at the details of the Delhi declaration. The declaration endorsed most of Iran’s main diplomatic concerns without speaking a single word against its drone and missile attacks on its neighboring Gulf states. There was likewise no mention of Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels, who have in recent times increased attacks on Saudi Arabia and held sea trade across the Red Sea hostage. The presence of Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan and his meeting with the Iranian president did not yield any tangible result, which India could have hailed as a diplomatic success of its foreign policy. Instead, India urged “maximum restraint” in West Asia.
The other clear shift in Indian foreign policy was seen in the absence of any mention of Israel’s “right to defend itself.” On the contrary, Israel was explicitly named and told to withdraw its forces from Lebanese territory. The declaration demanded unrestricted humanitarian aid to Gaza and opposed the forced displacement of Palestinians. The wording of the declaration may ruffle feathers in Israel when it says: “We reject any unilateral measures that seek to alter the legal and historical status of occupied Jerusalem. We urge full respect for the sanctity of all religious sites and holy places in the city and for the rights of all to access and to observe their religious rites without hindrance.”
The declaration referred to proceedings brought by South Africa against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
The declaration voiced deep concern over “deliberate attacks” on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities protected by U.N. atomic energy safeguards. The Associated Press described the provision as an indirect criticism of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear sites.
The remarkable turnaround in Indian foreign policy can be gauged from the fact that in many places Israel’s name is explicitly mentioned, whereas when it comes to Iran’s aggression, the language of diplomatic ambiguity is used.
Remember Modi’s language when he visited Israel in February 2026, where he was honored with a newly created Knesset medal? While addressing Indian-origin Jews, he said that “Israel is their fatherland and India their motherland,” highlighting their emotional bond to both. Within 48 hours of Modi’s visit, Israel and the U.S. launched aerial attacks on Iran.
What followed saw India dumping centuries-old ties with Iran into the Persian Gulf. India did not condemn the killing of more than 150 schoolgirls; Modi did not condemn or personally offer condolences for the assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and did not attend Khamenei’s funeral. All this was as India went increasingly Western, strengthening ties with Western and West Asian partners, especially Israel and the UAE. Despite all this, Iran kept diplomatic silence. But the entire scenario changed with Iran’s military success against the onslaught of the superior firepower of the U.S. and Israel.

articles.title: US Congressmen Call for Tougher Actions Against Key Southeast Asian Scam Enablers
articles.full_text:
Brian Mast (R-FL) and John Moolenaar (R-MI) have requested probes into 28 people and entities allegedly connected to scam gangs in Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar.
Two leading U.S. congressmen have called on the Trump administration to undertake further investigations into Southeast Asia’s scam industry, claiming that government-led crackdowns are leaving many important enablers untouched.
The request was conveyed in a letter by Brian Mast (R-FL), chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and John Moolenaar (R-MI), chairman of the Select Committee on China, dated Tuesday. In the letter, which was addressed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent, the pair requested further actions to combat scam operations in Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar.
In particular, Mast and Moolenaar requested a probe of 28 individuals and entities who have been accused of involvement in online scamming operations in the three nations, asking for a determination within 180 days as to whether they “meet the statutory criteria for imposition of sanctions” under U.S. law. The list includes businesspeople and government officials, including two sitting Cambodian ministers.
“Americans are being scammed online at enormous and still growing rates, due primarily to a network of Chinese transnational criminal organizations based in Southeast Asia,” the two congressmen wrote. “These sanctions investigations would significantly degrade the financial, business, and political structures in Southeast Asia complicit in online scams that have scammed Americans out of tens of billions of dollars annually.”
Online scamming operations have proliferated across mainland Southeast Asia since the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in loosely regulated parts of Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar. Coordinated predominantly by Chinese organized crime syndicates, these industrial-scale scam operations run romance-investment and crypto scams that target victims across the globe.
In addition to victimizing those on the receiving end of the scams, these operations rely on a large, indentured workforce – mostly ordinary people who have been trafficked or lured under false pretenses and held against their will. Inside scam centers, victims have reported being confined in cell-like rooms and subjected to beatings, mistreatment, and torture.
The Congressional request comes after a year in which authorities in Myanmar and Cambodia, under growing outside pressure, particularly from the United States and China, have launched well-publicized crackdowns on scam operations.
These have supposedly led to the demolition of the massive KK Park and Shwe Kokko scam hubs in Myanmar’s Karen State, and the eradication of online scam compounds in Cambodia – at least if Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who heads the government’s ad hoc Commission for Combating Online Scams, is to be believed.
Whether these crackdowns have gone far enough remains, however, a very open question. A report released yesterday by the Washington-based National Democratic Institute highlighted the extent to which transnational crime and formal structures of governance have become interleaved.
According to the report, which was authored by Jacob Sims, a visiting fellow at Harvard University and columnist for The Diplomat who specializes in Southeast Asia’s scam economy, wrote that by early 2026, scamming operations “had become a massive source of income for both the transnational syndicates and a set of elite co-perpetrators atop Cambodia’s party-state.”  This included “the ruling Hun family, many powerful party-state elites, and the formal institutions under their collective control.”
In their letter to Rubio and Bessent, Mast and Moolenaar cited abundant evidence claiming that “corrupt” senior government officials in Cambodia, Myanmar, and Laos have “turned a blind eye to this criminal activity at a shocking scale.” They also expressed concerns that few, if any, would likely be held to account, given that past crackdowns in these countries have “been largely performative.”
“While in recent months some regional governments have increased pressure on the scam industry, the financial networks, organizers, and political protection structures that enable it remain largely intact,” they wrote. “Impunity for perpetrators remains the norm.”
Among the most prominent figures listed in their letter was Cambodian Interior Minister Sar Sokha. Sokha was reportedly a former director of Jin Bei (Cambodia) Investment Co. Ltd., a firm that has developed casinos and scam centers in the port city of Sihanoukville, and has since been sanctioned by the U.S., the United Kingdom, and the European Union. Sokha has denied any involvement with scam operators and has hired two U.S. law firms to help keep him off the Treasury Department’s sanctions list.
Also on the list was Vorapak Tanyawong, a former Thai deputy finance minister who resigned in October after the publication of a report claiming that he had received $3 million in cryptocurrency from a Chinese-Cambodian criminal network. This network was allegedly connected to Benjamin Mauerberger (aka Ben Smith), a South African national who is alleged to be at the center of a complex financial web involving a number of prominent Cambodian and Thai political figures, some of whom are linked to the online scamming industry.
Among the other prominent figures listed in the congressional letter were Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister Neth Savoeun; deputy Cambodian police chief Dy Vichea (also a son-in-law of former Prime Minister Hun Sen); and Hun To, a cousin of Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet who has acknowledged owning a 30 percent share in Huione Pay PLC, a digital payments platform sanctioned by the U.S. government for alleged money laundering and ties to transnational scam operations.
Whether or not the letter produces any action by the Trump administration remains uncertain. In the cases of both Myanmar and Cambodia, rising awareness of the industrial scale of the online scamming problem has coincided with a realist turn in U.S. policy toward both countries, and particularly toward Cambodia, aimed at counterbalancing Chinese influence.
The U.S. government has already sanctioned a number of well-connected Cambodian businesspeople, including Ly Yong Phat, Kok An, and Chen Zhi, the chairman of the tentacular Prince Group, for their involvement in online scams. However, it currently has a strong diplomatic incentive to avoid directly implicating sitting government officials and other close allies of Hun Manet in the scam economy.
The most likely outcome is that Washington will accept the Cambodian government’s crackdown claims at face value in the interests of maintaining stable relations with Phnom Penh.

articles.title: Indian, Pakistani Naval Vessels Collide in Arabian Sea, Prompting Diplomatic Tensions
articles.full_text:
This is the first time since the May 2025 military clashes that tension between the two sides has erupted into the open.
On September 15, PNS Hunain, a Pakistan Navy corvette, collided with an Indian Navy warship, INS Kolkata, in the north Arabian Sea, 220 kilometers east of Oman. The following day, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) summoned Pakistan’s top-most diplomat in New Delhi, Chargé d’Affaires Saad Ahmad Warraich, to the foreign ministry to protest the “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct” of ​Pakistani naval units.
“While the incident, which took place in international waters, did not cause any major damage, the conduct of the Pakistani naval ship was in direct contravention of Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements of April 1991,” the MEA said in a statement.
Article 10 of the 1991 Agreement, which Pakistan reportedly flouted, states that naval ships and submarines belonging to the two countries should not come within three nautical miles of each other while operating in international waters. The agreement was signed as a confidence-building measure to put in place mechanisms for India and Pakistan to inform each other about military exercises or troop movements to prevent a crisis from arising due to the misreading of the other side’s intentions. It came following heightened tension when India conducted Brass Tacks, a massive military exercise in the states of Punjab and Rajasthan along the India-Pakistan border, in January 1987.
Meanwhile, across the border in Pakistan, the response mirrored that of India, with Islamabad blaming India for the incident. “While the Pakistan Navy was undertaking its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26, the Indian vessel carried out aggressive maneuvers in dangerously close proximity to a Pakistani naval ship, resulting in contact between the two vessels, ” the Pakistan Foreign Office said in a statement.
While the MEA described the incident as a collision, unnamed officials “aware of the matter” said that “it involved a close-in maneuvering by the Pakistani vessel, which approached the Indian warship at high speed and in an unsafe manner,” Hindustan Times reported. Another report in First Post, citing “sources within India’s defense establishment” claimed that “the Pakistani vessel shadowed the Indian ship, ignored multiple warnings and then made a high-speed crossing directly in front of the bow, resulting in the crash.”
A report in The Hindu, which cited sources in the defense ministry, said that INS Godavari was “on a routine surveillance mission,” when PNS Hunain “approached the Indian vessel while attempting to intercept or follow it. The close-range maneuver caused the two vessels to graze each other.” The Pakistani vessel “sustained damage in the collision and returned to the harbor. As for INS Godavari it “suffered minor damage and continued on its mission.”
Indian and Pakistani naval vessels last collided in 2011, when Pakistan’s PNS Babur “brushed past” INS Godavari in the Gulf of Aden, causing minor damage to the Indian warship’s helicopter safety net and triggering diplomatic tension.
Following the latest collision, both India and Pakistan summoned the charge d’affaires of the other side to lodge strong protests and have also asked their own charge d’affaires in the other country to register complaints with the government.
“Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents,” the MEA statement said.

articles.title: Who Is to Blame for the Massive Death Toll in the Nepal Floods?
articles.full_text:
The problem wasn’t China or a lack of data; it was Nepal’s lack of follow-through.
People gather to look at the damage after a massive flood in the Bhotekoshi River in Nuwakot, Nepal, Aug. 28, 2026.
When a massive flood hit Nepal on August 26, Nepali social media split almost immediately into two camps of grief and anger. One camp blamed the government of China, saying hundreds of Nepalis – over 1,400 as of the last count – died because the warning had simply failed. Commentators accused China of sitting on satellite and disaster monitoring data that could have bought Nepal precious minutes of warning. 
A second, more painful narrative came from survivors and local officials themselves: yes, the word had reached them that flood was coming down. There simply wasn’t enough time to react before the disaster arrived. 
China’s embassy in Kathmandu called the claims that it had withheld information “completely false and misleading,” insisting Beijing shared information with the Nepali side in time. But the strongest pushback on the blame narrative didn’t come from Beijing at all, but from Nepal’s own disaster authority, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA). 
“There have been several discussions. Actually, Chinese approached the Nepal government several times,” NDRRMA director Dr Prakash Pokhrel told me. “The Nepali side needs to be more proactive to finalize the data sharing agreement.” In other words, the problem wasn’t China refusing to share data. It was Nepal not following through. 
Days after the flood, researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment published a technical reconstruction of the disaster. They found that a glacier in Langtang Lirung’s south slope, at roughly 5,200 meters in elevation, had fractured at 10:52 a.m. China time (8:47 a.m. in Nepal), sending an ice-rock avalanche that scoured downhill and grew into a debris flow. It covered 22 kilometers and reached Gyirong Port on the Chinese side of the border in about seven minutes, an average speed of nearly 50 meters a second. 
Researchers said the debris was moving fast enough to leave people almost no time to react regardless of what anyone knew in advance. Chinese Academy of Sciences researcher Su Pengcheng attributed the collapse to long-term glacier instability driven by climate warning, not to any specific weather pattern that could have been tracked and disclosed in advance.   
Three weeks after the disaster, Nepal’s disaster authorities are still revising the death toll upward, with over 1,400 bodies recovered and 6,000 still missing on the Nepali side alone. Dozens more are dead or missing in Tibet. The disaster might not be over. A barrier lake at the collapse site remains, according to both governments, and a second flood is still possible.
Arguments over who knew what and when still continue, but the ongoing debate is hiding harder questions: can Nepal actually monitor hazards like this in real time on its own terms? Or does it keep failing at early warning in disaster after disaster because Nepal depends on satellite and monitoring infrastructure – none of which Nepal owns itself? 
Nepal is fast becoming one of the world’s most disaster-exposed regions, and that makes the question of sovereign space and monitoring capacity impossible to keep deferring. Satellite systems underpin flood warnings, cyclone alerts, navigation, communication, and climate monitoring functions on which the safety of hundreds of millions of people across the Himalayan region now depend. 
The August 26 flood and landslide was the third major glacier-linked disaster to hit almost exactly this region in roughly 14 months. In May 2025, two glacial lakes above Tilgau village in Humla burst. There was no rainfall recorded at all; the flood was purely a glacial trigger. 
In July 2025, a super glacial lake atop the Purepu Glacier drained into same Lende River hit by the August 2026 flood, The July 2025 event killed at least nine people in Nepal with 19 more missing. It destroyed the same Miteri Bridge at Rasuwagadhi and damaged the same hydropower plants and highways that August’s flood would later hit again. Chinese researchers later reconstructed that event too. According to imagery from China’s Gaofen-7 satellite, the lake had expanded more than sevenfold in two months before it burst. 
All three disasters involved the same tributary system, the same border, and the same fundamental problem. More importantly, all were monitored by excellent forensic satellite science, but the warning signs weren’t shared with people on the ground before the disaster.
That was true with the August 26 flood as well. Researchers using Sentinel-1 radar data found the glacier rock mass was speeding up a week before it actually broke. None of that imagery helped anyone evacuate. 
Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology wasn’t notified until roughly 9:00 a.m., about 20 minutes after the flood had begun. Remember, the debris flowed reached Gyirong in just seven minutes. By the time Nepal’s government was aware of the diaster, most of the communication towers in the area were already gone and officials had shifted to door-to-door warnings. 
The evacuation also failed because Nepal’s warning architecture could only react once a hazard had already reached the first river gauge downstream – and this time, the gauge was destroyed before it had time to register a flood. Nepal’s gauges measure water height, not how fast the water rises and this avalanche-driven surge rose far faster than the system was built to detect. As each station was destroyed while still showing normal levels, the flood went unnoticed until it reached Malekhu. 
Early Warning Infrastructure Nepal Doesn’t Own
To truly see the next flood coming, Nepal needs access to satellite imagery. If the disaster authority could monitor the condition of glaciers and glacial lakes, the country would know which areas are in danger. But that’s a tall order for Nepal, as NDRRMA director Pokhrel noted. Building Nepal’s own satellite, he told me, is “ambitious and very expensive.” 
A more realistic step for now is paying for clear satellite images that catch specific mountainsides destabilizing in real time. Nepal’s free access to Landsat and Sentinel doesn’t cover this. Those satellites give moderate resolution images and revisit a given slope only every five to 16 days. 
What Pokhrel wants is the other tier: high resolution, frequently revised commercial imagery, which Nepal currently only gets for free after a disaster through emergency mechanisms like Corpernicus’s Emergency Mapping Service. Nepal has no access to these images before a disaster, when it could actually help. 
As it stands, Nepal’s operational forecasting tools are largely built and hosted by other countries. Nepal’s International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) implements the SERVIR-HKH program, a joint initiative with NASA, the U.S. space agency, and USAID. SERVIR-HKH developed the Flash Flood Prediction Tool that feeds into Nepal’s warning along with a NASA Goddard-built landslide forecasting model piloted for the Karnali basin. 
But then the Trump administration pushed for cuts, and USAID stopped funding the project months before the disaster. Even then, the project wasn’t a full warning system. It was only providing data for Nepal’s own agencies to use. So, it is impossible to say with certainty that it would have changed the death toll. 
What is certain is that the tools Nepal relies on for exactly this kind of hazard monitoring were never sovereign to begin with. That’s what the SERVIR-HKH examples really highlights: that a decision made in a foreign capital can undermine Nepal’s disaster warning capabilities. 
Nepal’s own space capacity has never been enough for disaster early warning. Nepal has launched a handful of small satellites and Cubesat and holds two ITU geostationary orbital slots it has never developed. 
Even Existing Data Isn’t Being Used Effectively 
It would be tempting to conclude the fix is simply more satellites – either Nepal’s own or, as Pokhrel suggested, paid access to existed satellites’ image output. A peer-reviewed study published this year in Remote Sensing (MDPI) uses Nepal as a central case study to complicate that framing considerably. Legal access to satellite data is only the first of three conditions that must be fulfilled before that data can protect anyone. The other two are technical usability and institutional integration, which are precisely where Nepal falls short. 
Nepal already has free and legal access to Landsat, Sentinel, and MODIS imagery, even if those images are moderate resolution and on a fixed schedule. But Nepal lacks the domestic capacity to convert that imagery into a warning before, not after, a disaster. 
Citing World Bank data, the paper noted only 51.6 percent of Nepalis had internet access in 2024. More than half of secondary schools, and one in eight ward offices, were completely offline. A single Sentinel-2 image tile runs over 600 megabytes. Downloading that file is operationally impractical for a district office in a rural area. 
The same study points to the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology’s own flood forecasting tool, which was built with SERVIR-HKH, as a perfect example of this problem. Even years after it was introduced, it is still only used as a backup, not as the main tool for issuing warnings. And the program that built and maintained it, SERVIR-HKH, officially shut down in January 2025, so it’s unclear who is keeping it running now.
articles.summary: The problem wasn’t China or a lack of data; it was Nepal’s lack of follow-through.

articles.title: Malaysian PM Offers to Host Myanmar’s President in Refugee Repatriation Push
articles.full_text:
The country would be the fifth member of ASEAN to roll out of the red carpet for Min Aung Hlaing since his inauguration as president in April.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim speaks with reporters prior to his return from a state visit to the Maldives, Sep. 15, 2026.
Malaysia is set to welcome Myanmar’s military-appointed president for an official visit, in a bid to expedite the return of thousands of Rohingya Muslim refugees.
Speaking on a podcast yesterday, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said that he had invited Min Aung Hlaing to the country, on the condition that Myanmar agrees to take back citizens currently in Malaysia.
“I invited him to say we can be friends, ​we can trade, we can accept Myanmar, but Myanmar must accept them [the refugees] back,” Reuters reported.
If the trip eventuates, Malaysia will become the fifth member state of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to host Min Aung Hlaing since he took office in April, after trips to Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam. It will also become the first nation from maritime Southeast Asia to take such a step.
The six maritime ASEAN states – Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei, and Timor-Leste – have generally been more critical of Myanmar’s military than the nations of the mainland, since the coup of 2021.
Malaysia in particular has been one of the most outspoken, repeatedly expressing frustration at the Myanmar military’s refusal to cease hostilities and counseling a harder ASEAN line.
Anwar said yesterday that Malaysia was not ready to recognize Myanmar’s new government, ⁠but needed an authority to negotiate with on returning refugees.
“To me, that’s better diplomacy than just shouting angrily at Myanmar. Who’s going to take them? Where do we ‌send ‌them? They don’t even have Myanmar citizenship,” he said. “We, following ASEAN, don’t want direct relations with Myanmar. So who are we ‌supposed to negotiate with?”
While Malaysia’s hard line on Myanmar has softened somewhat over the past year, Anwar is under pressure to respond to the growing public hostility toward the Rohingya in Malaysia.
Large numbers of Rohingya have come to the country since 2017, when the Myanmar military launched an ethnic cleansing campaign that pushed more than 740,000 from their homes in Rakhine State into Bangladesh. Around 126,000 Rohingya asylum seekers are currently registered with the U.N. refugee agency in Kuala Lumpur, around half of the agency’s total, although Malaysia does not recognize them as refugees.
While the Rohingya were initially welcomed by their co-religionists, public opinion has soured in recent years as the population has continued to grow. During the course of 2026, in particular, Rohingya have faced an upsurge of xenophobic rhetoric and public hostility, particularly online.
This has put pressure on Malaysia’s government to advance long-stalled talks aimed at the refugees’ repatriation. The country’s immigration authorities have already reached a deal with Naypyidaw for the “voluntary” repatriation of some 5,000 refugees, which make up around half of the 10,388 Myanmar nationals currently being held at immigration detention depots.
The first 1,476 of this group is scheduled to return to Myanmar on September 29 aboard two Myanmar Navy warships and a hospital ship. In announcing the repatriation, the Ministry of Home Affairs stated that the refugees’ presence had become a “major financial burden, caused serious social problems, and created a real security threat to the country.”
Anwar said yesterday that the government was ultimately planning to send back 200,000 people, and that this could be carried out in stages if Myanmar was unable to receive all of them at once.
“If they cannot take 200,000 at one go, take them back in stages and we will help resolve it,” he said.
While the Malaysian side is narrowly focused on reaching a deal on refugees, Myanmar likely has wider diplomatic goals in mind. Since taking office in April, Min Aung Hlaing has been on a regional charm offensive aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of foreign investment to revive Myanmar’s war-damaged economy. This has involved state visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, and also to the four mainland ASEAN member states.
In particular, he has prioritized the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Since late 2021, the bloc has excluded the country from its summits over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus conflict resolution plan. This plan calls for a cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and inclusive dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
While Myanmar will no doubt seek to milk the Malaysia invitation for maximum legitimacy – a presidential spokesperson said this week that these countries “fully support Myanmar’s resumption of its active engagement in ASEAN as before” – the success of refugee repatriations remains very much in doubt.
The first question is whether the returns will be in any way “voluntary.” The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) has already expressed concerns about the September 29 repatriation, saying that the ongoing conflict and repression made it difficult to guarantee refugees’ safe return.
“Under customary international law – a binding obligation on all states – no one should be sent ​to a country where their rights or freedoms may be ​at risk,” UNHCR told Reuters last month. “Any refugee return must be voluntary, based on an informed decision, ‌and ⁠take place in conditions of safety and dignity.”
The second issue is whether the Naypyidaw government even has the authority to negotiate the return of Rohingya to Rakhine State. Most of the state is now under the control of the Arakan Army (AA), an ethnic Rakhine nationalist organization that is fighting for – and, since late 2023, has largely achieved – autonomy from the central state. This includes the northern townships of Maungdaw and Buthidaung, where a large proportion of Rohingya formerly lived.
How these refugees are to be returned remains very much an open question. A recent Myanmar military offensive aimed at seizing back territory from the AA around the state capital of Sittwe appears to have ground to a halt, leaving the central state with precarious footholds in Rakhine.

articles.title: Kazakhstan Again Sentences Activists for Supposed Attempt to Seize Power
articles.full_text:
Human rights organizations are speaking out after five Kazakh activists were convicted for an alleged plan to seize the presidential residence in Astana.
On September 8, five men were sentenced to between five and five-and-a-half years in prison after standing trial in an Almaty courtroom for supposedly attempting to seize control of power in Kazakhstan last year. The judges found all five suspects guilty not only of advocating for the violent seizure of power, but also of organizing mass unrest against authorities in the country and a seizure of the presidential residence, known as Akorda.
Several of the convicted have a past in activism, having taken part in multiple civil protests in the country over the years. While doors were closed for the hearings, the case sparked some attention from both activists and national human rights organizations. Along with criticizing the verdict, focus was also given to similar cases that had targeted activists previously. These types of court cases, activists argue, are part of a strategy employed by the Kazakh government to control opposition in the country.
While all of the defendants, aged between 56 and 62, were found guilty of advocating for mass riots and the seizure of power in Kazakhstan, two were found to have committed additional offenses. Kaisar Ozbek and Talgat Ashirov were convicted of illegally acquiring and storing explosives in relation to the unrest. These charges originally led the state prosecutor to request eight years in prison for each of the defendants.
When the trial began in February, the five men all entered not guilty pleas to all of the charges. Speaking with RFE/RL at the start of the trial, lawyers representing two of the defendants stated that their clients were simply ordinary people coerced into committing crimes.
Zhanara Balgabaeva, lawyer of one of the defendants, claimed that security forces made use of plants who pretended to share the activists’ views, then provoked them into committing crimes. “The civil activists, under the influence of these provocateurs, engaged in destructive conversations and activities of which my client was unaware,” she told RFE/RL.
She further criticized the decision to let the trial run behind closed doors, citing concerns for the rule of law: “They [the courts] don’t want transparency. They want to quickly shut everyone down without any fuss.”
This newest case taps into a trend of activists being accused of attempting to incite mass unrest or directly seize power in Kazakhstan. Such charges have now landed at least 17 people in prison since 2024. The Kazakhstan International Bureau of Human Rights and Rule of Law has questioned the neutrality of the country’s judicial system as a result. They suspect that the cases are a tactic employed by the Kazakh authorities to silence political adversaries.
The best known instance is often referred to as “the tractor case” due to the court claim that the seven charged activists planned to drive a tractor into Akorda in 2022. This supposedly would have been done in order to cause unrest in the country in an effort to seize power.
Another such case was presented in court just last year. In that case, five activists were sentenced to four years of restricted freedom for allegedly attempting to organize mass unrest in the country in relation to the referendum on the use of nuclear power in 2024. As suspects were interrogated in relation to this case, one defendant later stated that he was asked about their intention to seize control of Akorda in connection to the supposed plans of mass unrest.
Similar to the most recent case of an alleged plan to seize power, these previous incidents also included defendants of retirement age accused of planning mass unrest. Zhanara Balgabaeva, who has had a client in all three abovementioned cases, has also previously criticized the way evidence had been collected, pointing to some of it being acquired through provocations.
“In the ‘tractor case,’ when we were defending our clients, we said that any actions carried out through provocations are not admissible as evidence. Now we are seeing the same thing,” the lawyer stated in relation to the case surrounding the nuclear referendum.
With the recent verdict against five activists, Kazakhstan has now imprisoned activists for allegedly planning unrest for the third straight year, prompting both lawyers and human rights organizations to call foul play. Whether their criticism will have any effect on the Kazakh judicial system going forward remains to be seen.

articles.title: Siddhant Kishore on BRICS and the New Geopolitics of Asia
articles.full_text:
Siddhant Kishore joins host Tushar Shetty to examine the BRICS summit in New Delhi and the strategic realignment underway across Asia.
In this episode of Beyond the Indus, Siddhant Kishore, a New Delhi and Washington D.C.-based national security and foreign policy analyst, and former analyst at the Institute for the Study of War, joins host Tushar Shetty to examine the BRICS summit in New Delhi and the strategic realignment underway across Asia. 
They discuss the consensus preserved in the New Delhi Declaration and India’s diplomatic win on Pahalgam, the tactical stabilization between New Delhi and Beijing and why it falls short of realignment, the costly Iran-U.S. stalemate and Washington’s undefined war aim, the Houthi advance on the Bab al-Mandeb and the reconstitution of Iran’s proxy network, the operational hollowness of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, and the hedging by U.S. allies as Washington’s security commitments turn conditional.
For more in-depth analysis on South Asia, subscribe to the Beyond the Indus podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts, or follow us on YouTube for video episodes.
