articles.title: China and Mexico: How Far Should Technology Cooperation Go?
articles.full_text:
The Mexican government is deepening ties with Beijing in some of the sectors most sensitive to U.S. security concerns.
Rosaura Ruiz Gutiérrez, head of Mexico’s Secretariat of Science, Humanities, Technology, and Innovation (Secihti), shakes hands with Chinese Minister of Science and Technology Yin Hejun at the the Ninth Meeting of the Science and Technology Subcommittee of the Mexico-China Permanent Binational Commission, Sep. 6, 2026.
Between July and September 2026, scientific and technological cooperation between Mexico and China gained new momentum. Rosaura Ruiz Gutiérrez, head of Mexico’s Secretariat of Science, Humanities, Technology, and Innovation (Secihti), first met with Chinese Ambassador to Mexico Chen Daojiang and later co-chaired, alongside Chinese Minister of Science and Technology Yin Hejun, the Ninth Meeting of the Science and Technology Subcommittee of the Mexico-China Permanent Binational Commission. Since the mechanism was established in 2004, no Chinese minister of science and technology had personally participated in its meetings.
At the meeting, the two governments signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation among universities, public institutions, and companies in research, digital infrastructure, advanced technology transfer, and public-private partnerships. The areas discussed included artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, robotics, electromobility, and semiconductors. Secihti has also acknowledged that it is exploring opportunities to work with Huawei on high-performance computing, AI, and specialized talent development.
These developments come at a particularly difficult moment in Mexico’s relationship with the United States, which is spilling over into China-Mexico relations. 
Since January, the Mexican government has imposed new tariffs on 1,463 product categories originating in countries with which Mexico has no free trade agreement. Although China is not the only country affected, it has borne much of the impact: between January and May, Chinese imports covered by these measures fell by 28.4 percent. In sectors such as footwear and passenger vehicles, the declines reached 59 percent and 35 percent, respectively.
Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard has defended these measures as a way to protect Mexican industry. Yet they are difficult to separate from Washington’s pressure over China’s economic presence in Mexico and the upcoming USMCA review. On this issue, Claudia Sheinbaum’s government appears to have chosen to partially accommodate Trump in order to preserve an economic relationship that is exceedingly difficult to replace.
At the same time, Mexico has sought closer political ties with China amid poor treatment from the United States. On September 4, U.S. President Donald Trump declared from the Oval Office that Mexico had “nothing that we really need,” beyond “spicy tamales, tomatoes, a couple of things.” 
Just three days later, Mexico’s Foreign Secretary Roberto Velasco traveled to Beijing to meet with Wang Yi. There, the Chinese foreign minister expressed support for Mexico against “foreign interference” and argued that China-Mexico relations “are not directed at any third party and should not be affected by any third party.” Neither government explicitly mentioned the United States, but both appeared to have it very much in mind.
There is nothing inherently problematic about Mexico seeking to diversify its international relations. If anything, the uncertainty created by Trump demonstrates the risks of depending excessively on a single partner. But if the Mexican government is trying to reduce commercial frictions with Washington, how should we interpret its simultaneous deepening of ties with Beijing in some of the sectors most sensitive to U.S. security concerns?
Recent exchanges between Secihti and its Chinese counterparts reveal at least three particularly problematic areas. The first concerns the technologies chosen for deeper cooperation. Artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and high-performance computing – all explicitly discussed during these meetings – are not ordinary industries. They are at the heart of the China-U.S. competition to achieve greater technological autonomy, control supply chains, and preserve industrial and military advantages. Washington has therefore spent much of the past decade restricting China’s access to advanced chips and other dual-use technologies.
The second concerns Huawei. Before the Subcommittee meeting, Secihti itself announced that it was exploring cooperation with the Chinese company in high-performance computing, AI, and specialized talent development. Since the first Trump administration, Huawei has been at the center of U.S. restrictions on Chinese technology over security and espionage concerns. These concerns have even generated tensions between Washington and allied governments over Chinese companies’ participation in 5G networks and other digital infrastructure.
Finally, Secihti’s exchanges with Chinese representatives have placed considerable emphasis on student and researcher mobility, as well as cooperation among universities, research centers, and companies. Promoting these exchanges is perfectly legitimate and can yield real benefits. Yet when academic cooperation overlaps with dual-use technologies, it requires safeguards different from those of conventional academic exchange. The U.S. Congress has warned about ties between certain Chinese universities and scientific programs and Beijing’s “military-civil fusion” strategy, through which advances developed in civilian settings can contribute to military capabilities.
This does not make every Chinese student or researcher a security risk – a conclusion that would be both unfair and absurd. But it does require distinguishing between cooperation on agricultural pests – as the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) and the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences already do – and transferring knowledge related to semiconductors, AI, or high-performance computing. Precisely because Secihti’s new agenda encompasses both kinds of cooperation, Mexico should be able to tell the difference.
It is possible, of course, that many of these agreements will never reach the scale suggested by official statements. Latin America’s experience shows that many memorandums signed with China produce more declarations and photo opportunities than lasting projects. Even so, it is striking that the priorities discussed in Secihti’s exchanges closely resemble sectors promoted by Beijing’s industrial policy over the past decade, from Made in China 2025 to its policy documents on Latin America and the Caribbean.
Diversifying Without Creating New Dependencies
Mexico, then, faces a problem that has less to do with its right to cooperate with China than with the coherence of its international strategy. It is contradictory to limit China’s economic presence in order to reduce friction with Washington while simultaneously deepening ties with Beijing in sectors that are far more sensitive to the United States.
China, moreover, is not Mexico’s only option for diversification. The modernized Mexico-European Union Global Agreement would allow more than 95 percent of Mexican exports to enter tariff-free into a market of 450 million people. Mexico could also make better use of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) or revitalize the Pacific Alliance, whose enlargement has remained stalled, among other reasons, by the diplomatic rupture with Ecuador following the 2024 raid on the Mexican Embassy in Quito. More ambitious commercial ties with Mercosur could complement these efforts.
None of these alternatives will replace the United States – the destination of more than 80 percent of Mexican exports. Nor could China, for that matter. But stronger ties with Europe, the Asia-Pacific, and Latin America could gradually reduce Mexico’s dependence without placing the country in the middle of the most contentious areas of China-U.S. competition.
Autonomy does not mean replacing one dependency with another, much less antagonizing Washington simply to demonstrate that Mexico can do so. Maintaining close relations with China is perfectly compatible with an independent foreign policy, but Mexico cannot ignore the costs of cooperation in sensitive areas. Trading with China is not the same as partnering with Beijing on digital infrastructure, semiconductors, or artificial intelligence. In an era of great power competition, diversification requires knowing not only whom to engage with, but also how far – and in what areas – to do so.

articles.title: In Turkmenistan’s Data Desert, the Golden Age Is a Mirage
articles.full_text:
The IMF says Turkmenistan, in failing to provide key economic data, is in breach of its obligations.
It was a short press release, published on a Friday afternoon and easily missed. 
The International Monetary Fund’s executive board had considered a report on “Turkmenistan’s observance of its obligations… which requires member countries to provide data necessary for the IMF’s activities.” 
Ashgabat, the board said, “has not provided key required data, including information on international reserve assets, official holdings of gold and foreign exchange, and a complete balance of payments.”
This non-provision, the statement continued, “could not be explained by a lack of capacity and therefore constitutes a breach of Turkmenistan’s obligations.” In six months, the board will consider again Turkmenistan’s progress, the statement said, noting that the provision of data helps the IMF support effective policy formation.
The IMF probably shouldn’t hold its proverbial breath.
“This is not something new,” Aynabat Yaylymova, executive director of the Progres Foundation told The Diplomat. “Concealing information is a key to a regime’s survival.”
The Progres Foundation works with Turkmen experts to monitor, research, and highlight human development in Turkmenistan in absence of reliable government data or adequate government attention.
Keen readers of the regular World Bank Global Economic Prospects reports will have noted that for years, footnotes touch on Turkmenistan’s exclusion from various data sets. In 2021, one such report noted: “Due to lack of reliable data of adequate quality, the World Bank is currently not publishing economic output, income, or growth data for Turkmenistan and República Bolivariana de Venezuela.”
A 2024 World Bank publication titled “Turkmenistan Economic Report” explained via a highlighted box buried at the end of the report that, “Turkmenistan provides limited trade data publications, compounded by concerns about the reliability of Turkmenistan’s official statistics.” The box went on to explain how the analysts triangulated trade statistics for the country via the mirrored data sets of 109 other countries, but noted that this method has its own failings – especially since Russia and Belarus no longer share trade data either. 
In March 2018 the IMF issued a declaration of censure against Venezuela, in light of its failure to take action on a November 2017 warning that mirrors the notice issued last week to Turkmenistan. Since Venezuela was not, at the time, actively borrowing from the IMF the censure had little bite. 
“I am not sure the IMF has leverage in this case since the government does not use its financial resources,” Yaylymova commented. “The government also does not care about its reputation.”
Ashgabat joined the IMF in 1992 but has engaged only marginally, never taking part in any assistance or borrowing programs. Doing so would undercut the myth the Turkmen government repeats ad nauseum: Turkmen are living in a golden age. 
“Turkmenistan’s story since independence is the story of the government that operates with impunity and extreme opacity,” Yaylymova explained. 
When The Diplomat asked why Turkmenistan is so recalcitrant with its data, Yaylymova said that, “Providing the IMF with a complete, verifiable balance of payments and official reserve data would force the government to expose exactly where the billions from the sales of natural gas are held, how they are managed, and how they are spent. This is in the context where citizens have never seen the state budget.”
Turkmenistan’s state news platform is named “Altyn Asyr” – “Golden Age” – and ostentatiously hopeful language pervades government statements, regardless of the actual reality of life in Turkmenistan. 
“If the government provides the data requested by the IMF,” Yaylymova continued, “it will officially dismantle the autocratic regime’s domestic propaganda narrative and expose the true state of the economy to both its citizens, international community, and markets.”
According to the Turkmen government, the growth rate sits at 6.3 percent – around where it has been since 2015. Not even the COVID-19 pandemic dented Turkmenistan’s officially reported growth rate. But, according to Ashgabat, in Turkmenistan there was no COVID-19 pandemic.
“During COVID… Turkmens counted graves to understand the level of infection,” Yaylymova said, noting that there are always indirect ways of understanding reality in the absence of data. 
“In economic mismanagement and grand corruption we should look at deeply neglected human potential and increased migration out of the country.”
Earlier this month, RFE/RL’s Turkmen Service, Radio Azatlyk, reported that young people who previously studied abroad were being prevented from leaving the country. This isn’t new either.
“It is crucial to understand the domestic context. Poverty is deepening in Turkmenistan,” Yaylymova told The Diplomat.
The Progres Foundation publishes a unique economic index, the Palaw Index, which tracks inflation via the ingredients of palaw, the national dish of Turkmenistan comprised of beef, oil, onions, carrots, and rice, known elsewhere as plov, osh, or pilaf. According to the April/June 2026 index, the average cost of making the dish in the capital city reached 91.4 Turkmen manat ($26.16), a 29.4 percent jump from the same period in 2025. The increase was driven primarily by a sharp rise in beef prices which the analysis attributes to “substantial livestock losses – particularly in the Ahal region – caused by drought, malnutrition, and disease.”
None of that was reported in Turkmen state media.
On September 14, however, one headline announced that “The National Leader of the Turkmen people, Chairman of the Halk Maslakhaty of Turkmenistan, Hero-Arkadag, got acquainted with the progress of the second stage of the new city and the developed projects,” in reference to Turkmenistan’s top leader, Gurbanguly Berdimehamedov – father of the current president, Serdar Berdimehamedov – and the bespoke smart city being built for an estimated $5 billion that bears his nickname, meaning “protector.”
Turkmenistan ranks fourth globally in terms of proven gas reserves, sitting between Qatar and Saudi Arabia. An estimated 90 percent of its gas exports go to China for unknown billions in revenue. But Turkmen citizens and international financial institutions alike don’t know exactly where the money goes.
“The public has no idea where the revenues from natural resources go,” Yaylymova told The Diplomat. “In an authoritarian and kleptocratic regime such as Turkmenistan data means accountability, it means that someone is going to keep you accountable by questioning your data, logic, and assumptions and what you do or you do not do.”
An absence of data is an absence of accountability. It “enables economic mismanagement, arbitrary and opaque rule,” Yaylymova said.
The IMF may lack leverage over Turkmenistan, but censure, Yaylymova said, is nevertheless long overdue.
“The government keeps exaggerating the growth rate while the population is plunging deeper into despair and poverty,” she stressed. It’s important, she concluded, for international organizations and Turkmenistan’s partners to “start naming the structural issues” directly and start “calling on the government publicly to meet its obligations.”
articles.summary: The IMF says Turkmenistan, in failing to provide key economic data, is in breach of its obligations.

articles.title: What Malaysia’s Recent State Election Results Say About the Country’s Political Direction
articles.full_text:
Oh Ei Sun of the Singapore Institute of International Affairs discusses the outcome of the recent elections in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
Supporters of the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition rally in Negeri Sembilan ahead of state elections, July 31, 2026.
The Malaysian states Johor and Negeri Sembilan recently held state elections that produced disappointing results for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s coalition.
During the July 11 polls in Johor, an economically important state at the tip of peninsular Malaysia, Barisan Nasional (BN), ​secured a commanding victory, winning 48 of 56 state assembly seats, up from 40 at the last election in 2022. Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition won the remaining eight seats, down from 12 previously.
This result was largely replicated in Negeri Sembilan on August 1. Here BN won 18 of the 36 seats in the state’s legislative assembly and was set to form government with the pan-Malay Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition, which won seven seats. PH, which had ruled the state in coalition with BN prior to the election, saw its share of seats drop from 17 to 11.
In both contests, the losses were particularly marked for the Democratic Action Party (DAP), a key member of the PH coalition that is traditionally associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese community. In Negeri Sembilan, the election was also marked by close cooperation between the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) and the Islamist party PAS, the primary components of the BN and PN coalitions, respectively. This has raised suggestions that a new “Malay wave” could be set to wash away Anwar’s coalition at the next general election.
The twist is that BN and PH remain in coalition at the federal level, following the close-run general election of 2022. The growing competition between the two nominal partners has even raised the possibility that Anwar may choose to call a snap election.
Dr. Oh Ei Sun, a senior fellow at the Singapore Institute of International Affairs, spoke to The Diplomat’s Southeast Asia Editor Sebastian Strangio recently about what the results might mean for Anwar’s leadership and federal politics as Malaysia moves toward its next general election.
Let’s start with the most obvious question: How do you interpret the collapse of PH’s position in Johor and Negeri Sembilan?
I think there are similarities and differences in some of the major factors that led to PH’s collapse in these two states. The similarities lie primarily in the voters’ seeming conflation of PH’s perceived performance (or non-performance) at the federal level with their political solicitation at the state level.
To be more specific, we may look closer into PKR [the People’s Justice Party] and DAP – PH’s two largest component parties – respectively but also relatedly. PKR’s core supporters are those seeking social and political reforms, ranging from those advocating revamp of parliamentary and electoral systems to those who are fervently against corruption and power abuses. Many of them have become increasingly impatient with what they perceived as PKR’s feet-dragging since coming to federal power at fulfilling its reform promises that were loudly proclaimed during its opposition years. Worse still, some of them saw regressive measures that were unashamedly touted, such as those controlling freedom of expression online, that were reminiscent of pre-2018 BN days.
At the same time, PKR at the government’s driver seat was also perceived to be at best lackluster in its microeconomic performance, with many members of lower- and even middle-income groups finding it hard to carry on with livelihood, a scenario that was perceived to be worse than the BN days. So these core PKR supporters carried this rather disgruntled attitude toward PKR from the federal to the state level, and did not come out in droves to support PKR. Yet PKR, with its same, reformist image, remained inept in competing with UMNO and PAS in attracting an increasingly conservative Malay voters cohort to make up or surpass the difference.
DAP shared many of these misgivings and thus non-votes by its core supporters as PKR, plus disillusion from its non-Malay core supporters who had even higher expectations of DAP championing their long-held dream of attaining political and social equality. When they perceived DAP as having been non-enthusiastic in advancing this dear cause of theirs since coming to federal power, and furthermore remained silent when their rights were perceived to have been trampled upon, they wanted to “punish” DAP by not voting for it.
But these conflated or “transferred” disfavors against PH aside, there were also respective distinct factors that favor BN in these two states. The Johor chief minister, Onn Hafiz, turned out to be both charismatic and pragmatic, having brought in large amounts of foreign investment into the state that were transforming the state’s economic outlook. So the voters were comfortable with his helmsmanship and would like to see him continue in his leading role. In Negeri Sembilan, UMNO and PAS non-contest arrangements prevented vote splitting and handed easy wins to UMNO and participation by PAS for the first time in the state administration. This was a win-win situation for both parties. How long the state ruling coalition could hold is quite another question, if past disastrous collaboration history between UMNO and PAS provides any lesson.
Do you anticipate a similar result in Melaka, the next state to hold an election?
The conflated or “transferred” disfavors against PH by its core supporters would most likely remain quite intact in Melaka, as nothing much is likely to take place within a space of at most a few months to dissuade them otherwise. On the other hand, the Onn Hafiz favorite-son factor is certainly missing in Melaka, which saw at best average socioeconomic performance over the last half decade. And it would appear that BN and the PAS-led PN could still not reach a no-contest agreement in Melaka. As such, PH could aspire to holding on to its present state seats in Melaka. Anything more would be a distinct bonus.
The Negeri Sembilan election in particular was marked by close cooperation between BN and PN (particularly between UMNO and PAS), which have recently been at loggerheads. This has prompted some to suggest that a “Malay wave” could wash away Anwar and PH at the next general election. Do you think this is likely, and if so, why?
I think a Malay-Muslim wave that would be swept to power remains a very viable political scenario, as it almost did in the last general election. This is due not so much to PAS’ or UMNO’s revitalized political or electoral prowess. Rather, it is an electoral manifestation of an increasingly vibrant Malay-Muslim desire to attain a much more conservative and religiously oriented social and political outlook for the country. This is in line with yet another wave of religious revivalism that is sweeping across many Muslim-majority countries, ranging from Turkey to Indonesia. So the majority of Malay voters see PAS as a most conducive political vehicle for the soonest realization of this earnest desire, with UMNO as perhaps second best in realizing so. Therefore, a PAS-UMNO electoral alliance is likely to trump PH hands down.
But ironically, Anwar may remain prime minister after the next general election. This is due to the power struggles that are taking place within UMNO and PAS, which are usually more intense than their confrontations with PH. UMNO’s internecine fights are mainly factional in nature, with different warlords and their power bases rallying against one another. So Zahid the party president may ultimately not be touted as a viable prime ministerial candidate, with his many unresolved legal cases as the pretext. The fights in PAS, on the other hand, are usually ideological in nature, pitching the conservative ulamas against the more moderate professionals. The ulamas would loath to see a moderate such as the much-mentioned Terengganu chief minister Shamsuri to become prime minister. So Anwar, with his sizable religious and communal credentials in the past, may actually emerge as a compromise figurehead prime minister with PAS and to a lesser extent UMNO pulling the string behind the scene.
PH and BN insist their federal ​partnership can co-exist with rivalries at the state level, but how sustainable is the current situation? Do you anticipate Anwar calling a GE any time soon?
Malaysia has entered a very fragmented political landscape, with perhaps no single party being able to command an outright parliamentary majority, thus necessitating the forming of ruling coalitions. So the main calculation for alliance or split is not so much an ideological one as a politically convenient one. Therefore, the answer to the sustainability of any political coalitions really depends on the electoral viability and the thirst for power of its potential component parties.
It really does not matter when Anwar would call for a general election. The Malay-Muslim wave will sweep aside a large portion of its PH, but he may remain politically useful as prime minister.
How do you interpret the collapse of the DAP vote in the two recent elections, and also the state election in Sabah in November? What does this say about the dynamics of ethnic Chinese politics in peninsular Malaysia? If the party decides to leave the PH coalition, what impact could that have on Anwar’s political chances at the next GE?
See particularly the answer to the first question above. But there is a bit of a nuance to DAP in Sabah. DAP was trounced in Sabah mainly because it aligned itself too closely to the state ruling coalition there that was evidently disfavored by DAP’s core Sabah supporters, who decided to pitch their tent with Warisan instead, which they thought would come back to power. Nationally, the non-Malays continue to aspire to a fairer and more equal Malaysia. DAP’s decision to remain in cabinet is likely to come back to haunt it in the general election, as it would have to continue to collectively shoulder the kind of decisions which non-Malays may perceive to be unfair and unequal.
The Malaysian states Johor and Negeri Sembilan recently held state elections that produced disappointing results for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s coalition.
During the July 11 polls in Johor, an economically important state at the tip of peninsular Malaysia, Barisan Nasional (BN), ​secured a commanding victory, winning 48 of 56 state assembly seats, up from 40 at the last election in 2022. Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition won the remaining eight seats, down from 12 previously.
This result was largely replicated in Negeri Sembilan on August 1. Here BN won 18 of the 36 seats in the state’s legislative assembly and was set to form government with the pan-Malay Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition, which won seven seats. PH, which had ruled the state in coalition with BN prior to the election, saw its share of seats drop from 17 to 11.
In both contests, the losses were particularly marked for the Democratic Action Party (DAP), a key member of the PH coalition that is traditionally associated with Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese community. In Negeri Sembilan, the election was also marked by close cooperation between the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) and the Islamist party PAS, the primary components of the BN and PN coalitions, respectively. This has raised suggestions that a new “Malay wave” could be set to wash away Anwar’s coalition at the next general election.
The twist is that BN and PH remain in coalition at the federal level, following the close-run general election of 2022. The growing competition between the two nominal partners has even raised the possibility that Anwar may choose to call a snap election.
Dr. Oh Ei Sun, a senior fellow at the Singapore Institute of International Affairs, spoke to The Diplomat’s Southeast Asia Editor Sebastian Strangio recently about what the results might mean for Anwar’s leadership and federal politics as Malaysia moves toward its next general election.
articles.summary: Oh Ei Sun of the Singapore Institute of International Affairs discusses the outcome of the recent elections in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.

articles.title: Pakistan-Oman Maritime Deal Signals Gwadar’s Expanding Regional Relevance
articles.full_text:
As the strategically located Pakistani port’s geopolitical value increases, can its market readiness keep pace?
Gwadar Port in Pakistan’s Balochistan province.
Pakistan and Oman are discussing a strategic maritime agreement to designate Pakistan’s Gwadar Port and Oman’s Sohar Port as sister ports. Pakistani officials say the agreement will help the two ports work more closely on operational matters and create fresh opportunities for trade and investment between the two countries.
This is the latest in a series of developments in recent months that have elevated Gwadar’s profile amid growing uncertainty over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, driven by the Iran-U.S. war.
Gwadar Port is located on Pakistan’s southwestern coast in Balochistan. It sits roughly 400 kilometers from the Strait of Hormuz. It is a deep-sea port developed primarily with Chinese financing and technical support under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The port is operated by the China Overseas Port Holding Company, which holds a long-term lease of 40 years, while the Gwadar Port Authority retains overall ownership and regulatory oversight of the project.
However, the port’s full operational realization faces persistent internal challenges. Security in the province of Balochistan remains volatile as militant groups continue to target infrastructure projects and foreign personnel. These ongoing insurgent threats have delayed commercial expansion, raised security costs, and created caution among international investors regarding long-term commitments.
Gwadar Port Authority Chairman Noor-ul-Haq Baloch said last week that the sister-port initiative is not just tied to the current disruptions or uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz but is part of Pakistan’s long-term strategic vision. Once finalized, the agreement would facilitate greater trade and collaboration between the two ports, he said. It would allow them to explore shared commercial opportunities. Moreover, discussions are also underway for potential Omani investments in the Gwadar Free Zone along with possible joint ventures in logistics, warehousing, and fisheries.
Furthermore, Baloch outlined several practical dimensions of the partnership. “First is the knowledge exchange about port operations. Second is mutual training of port officials. Third is if a shipping line is coming to Pakistan and Oman, the sister ports can collectively offer a discount to that particular line — this is called a commercial arrangement,” he explained. “Fourth is the operational aspect in which sister ports give priority to each other’s ships.”
Beyond Oman, Gwadar’s strategic potential rests on its role as an alternative transit route for other regional economies. Arguably, the idea of strengthening maritime links allows Pakistan to offer landlocked Central Asian countries the shortest overland access to international sea lanes.
In recent years, Pakistan has intensified diplomatic efforts to operationalize Gwadar by capitalizing on the harbor’s rising geopolitical importance. While Islamabad has been rolling out incentives for shipping lines and businesses seeking to diversify supply chains, Pakistan’s policymakers appear to be drawing on the port’s external linkages by leveraging the broader geopolitical environment.
Pakistan’s heightened attention to building on Gwadar’s external linkages began gathering momentum with the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022. Since then, proposals to link Gwadar with the Russia-backed International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) have been put forward. Russia is keen to secure alternative trade routes and warm-water access to the Arabian Sea amid Western sanctions and disruptions to its traditional European corridors. In May this year, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk confirmed that Moscow and Islamabad are discussing linking Gwadar Port with the INSTC.
Clearly, the Iran-U.S. conflict and the subsequent pressures on the Strait of Hormuz have prompted renewed international attention on Gwadar. Amid these developments, the port’s primary value appears to have emerged largely from geopolitical circumstances in the region and beyond.
Much of the discussion among Pakistani officials centers on the idea that Gwadar can provide alternative logistics and potential energy routing benefits during periods of regional instability. There is little focus on making infrastructure, connectivity and incentives that Gwadar is currently offering, or planning to offer, that would make it competitive or superior to those available at other ports across the region.
Pakistani officials need to align their efforts with the idea that regional instability in any form will not automatically translate into lasting economic gains for Gwadar. That said, the longer-term outlook for Gwadar remains promising in terms of its strategic attractiveness to major powers, particularly those in the Asia-Pacific region. The port clearly holds the potential to serve as an effective bridge linking Pakistan to western China, Central Asia, and, potentially, markets further afield in Africa.
The task before the Pakistani government is to act swiftly to address structural shortcomings so that the existing geopolitical opportunities can be transformed into durable economic value.

articles.title: Indonesia Replaces Finance Minister Amid Growing Investor Skepticism
articles.full_text:
The appointment of Suahasil Nazara, who has served as deputy finance minister since 2019, is intended to calm investors worried about Jakarta’s fiscal profligacy.
Suahasil Nazara, then Indonesia’s deputy finance minister, participates in a meeting in Bali, Indonesia, Aug. 10, 2025.
Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto has fired and replaced his finance minister, Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa, just over a year after his appointment.
Suahasil Nazara, 55, who has served as deputy finance minister since 2019, was yesterday sworn in as Purbaya’s replacement.
The government did not say why Purbaya was removed, but his year in the post has been marked by ructions in the Indonesian economy, including a sharp depreciation of the rupiah and growing investor skepticism.
After being sworn-in yesterday afternoon, Suahasil told the press that he had only learned about his appointment in the morning.
“This is, of course, an expression of the trust placed in me by the president and the country. I am grateful for that trust, and I hope I can carry out the responsibility entrusted to me by the president,” Suahasil said, as per the Jakarta Globe.
He added that Prabowo had instructed him to safeguard “the health and credibility” of the state budget.
The replacement of the finance minister comes after a turbulent year at the top echelons of Indonesia’s major economic institutions. In late July, Perry Warjiyo, the governor of Bank Indonesia, the country’s central bank, stepped down, two years before the expiry of his current term as BI governor.
Purbaya was appointed finance minister last September, after the resignation of Sri Mulyani Indrawati, who had served in the post under three presidents. While Sri Mulyani initially agreed to serve in the role under Prabowo after he took office in October 2024, she eventually was forced out, reportedly due to differences between her conservative economic approach and Prabowo’s fiscally expansive economic agenda. The Indonesian president has set an ambitious goal of 8 percent annual GDP growth for the rest of his term, and he introduced a number of high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, that have widened the fiscal deficit.
The removal of Sri Mulyani unsettled investors who were already unsure about Indonesia’s economic trajectory under Prabowo. The year since her departure has only compounded these concerns. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”
This came shortly after the global index provider MSCI threatened to downgrade Indonesia to “frontier market” status due to a number of transparency concerns in its stock market, including the high concentration of ownership in certain companies and the limited “free float” of shares. MSCI will announce its verdict in November.
At the same time, the rupiah has fallen to record lows this year, passing the psychological threshold of 18,000 rupiah to the U.S. dollar in June. A spike in ​the fuel subsidy budget following the rise in global crude prices has added to the deficit and pushed it toward its legally mandated ceiling of 3 percent of GDP.
Amid these various challenges, Purbaya’s tendency to veer off script – Channel News Asia described him yesterday as “brash and unfiltered” – has not helped calm investor sentiment. In April, Purbaya courted international controversy when he half-jokingly floated the idea of imposing a levy on ships passing through the Malacca Strait, describing it as a possible way that Indonesia could leverage its proximity to a key artery of global trade. The Foreign Ministry was subsequently forced to walk back his comments.
While the removal of Sri Mulyani was intended to align the Ministry of Finance with Prabowo’s economic goals, the cashiering of Purbaya appears to be aimed more at outside constituencies. According to the Financial Times, Suahasil “is seen as a technocrat and has extensive experience in fiscal policymaking, having previously led the country’s fiscal policy agency for more than three years.”
Reuters described the move as an attempt “to win back investor confidence amid long-festering concerns about policymaking and fiscal profligacy.” Richard Borsuk of Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International ​Studies told the news agency that Suahasil’s appointment was a “good move.” He said, “The market should like it and rating agencies would already know and like Nazara.”
Speaking yesterday, Suahasil said that he would ensure that the country’s fiscal deficit would be kept under the legal ceiling of 3 percent. “This is just a continuation, not a change… We will continue to manage the state’s finances in a better way,” he said.

articles.title: India-hosted BRICS Summit Steers Clear of Contentious Moves
articles.full_text:
The Delhi Declaration made no mention of de-dollarization. But it did back trade in national currencies.
Leaders of BRICS member nations plant banyan tree saplings to mark the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi, India, Sept 12, 2026.
The 18th BRICS summit hosted by India on September 12-13 criticized unilateral tariffs, sanctions, and protectionism in international trade, expressed support for multilateralism and multipolarity, and saw the airing of serious concern over rising tensions in West Asia.
The summit was being closely watched for several reasons. The first was whether the summit would produce a consensual joint statement. The second was curiosity over whether the BRICS members would collectively reject the dollar as the main currency of international trade. And third, to see what it could say about unilateral tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump, especially since Brazil and India, two BRICS founding members, were slapped with the highest tariff rate of 50 percent last year before they were reduced.
This was the first summit that India was hosting since its expansion in 2024. The presence of leaders from Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) – countries caught in the war in West Asia – at the same table in New Delhi also raised the scrutiny levels.
The summit produced a consensus outcome document, the “New Delhi Declaration.” It was not expected to do so; a BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in May ended without consensus, especially over words to describe the U.S. war on Iran and Tehran’s subsequent strikes on Gulf countries, including BRICS members. The Delhi Declaration expressed anguish over the situation in the Middle East without naming any of the parties – neither the U.S., Israel, Iran, nor any of the Gulf countries – involved in the conflict. It expressed “deep concern” over the “continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia” and called for “exercising maximum restraint” and “avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation.”
The statement supported a two-state solution to end Israel-Palestine tensions and called for the halt of the forced displacement of Palestinians. Comments on Palestine aren’t new for BRICS but acquire salience given the current situation in Gaza.
There was no mention of “de-dollarization” either, i.e., BRICS members reducing their reliance on the dollar for trade, financing, and as part of official reserves. Nor was there any reference to a BRICS common currency.
But BRICS did back intra-group commerce carried out in local currencies. This is not surprising given that Russia and Iran are under multiple layers of sanctions prohibiting trade in dollars or euros. Countries like India, which have been buying oil from Russia in the wake of the West Asia crisis, have been finding it difficult to pay for oil purchases.  The possibility that BRICS could sideline the dollar as an international trade currency has placed it in the crosshairs of the Trump administration.
BRICS has been seen as a counterweight to Western-led institutions and a platform for building an alternative international order, especially given the presence of countries like China and Russia. India, on its part, has made it clear that it is “non-West” but not “anti-West.” Participation in BRICS, as in the Australia-Japan-U.S.-India Quad forum, reinforces India’s multi-alignment strategy in an uncertain world.
At the summit’s opening, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi pointedly underlined that the grouping sought to move forward “not against anyone, but with an approach of taking everyone along.”
In New Delhi, BRICS reiterated its “commitment to strengthening multilateralism and multipolarity and to upholding international law” in the statement. The “proliferation of trade-restrictive actions” threatened global trade and disrupted global supply chains while introducing uncertainty into international economic and trade activities, it said. “We voice serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with WTO rules,” it added.
In his opening remarks, Modi said BRICS needed to chart out global reforms to secure a bigger voice for developing countries in global decision-making. The “pyramid of privilege” must be changed to a “platform of partnership,” he said.
“Ensuring equal participation in shaping the global rules of the future is of utmost importance. AI, cyberspace, outer space, biotechnology, and critical technologies are shaping not only the opportunities of the future, but also the rules that will govern the future,” Modi added. In the closing session on September 13, Modi raised concerns about the “weaponization of technology and critical minerals,” warning that it could hinder shared growth and development prospects.
At the opening session, China’s President Xi Jinping pitched BRICS as the world’s most influential grouping for cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries. He called on BRICS to strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence and encourage open-source development, cooperation and sharing. He invited BRICS countries to participate in the Shanghai-headquartered World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization set up in July and seen as China’s attempt to shape global AI governance, rivaling the U.S.’ Pax Silica. Xi also said Beijing was willing to work with BRICS countries to play a “due role” in bringing peace to the Middle East.
“We must oppose withdrawing from organizations, breaking treaties, and starting anew by setting up separate mechanisms,” Xi said, in what is seen as thinly veiled criticism of the U.S., which under Trump has walked out of pacts on climate change and many international organizations.
So, apart from a wordy 140-paragraph document, what did India achieve at the 18th BRICS summit?
“New Delhi’s diplomatic success lies in keeping BRICS ‘boring,’” in the middle of “rhetorical excess about radical global change,” security affairs analyst C Raja Mohan wrote in an opinion piece on September 13.
“The declaration reaffirms the political diversity of the forum and dispels the notion of an ideological crusade against the West — one that some supporters of BRICS desire and many of its critics assume is already under way,” he wrote.
The summit’s “principal achievement is to underline a simpler proposition: a more fragmented world requires more, not less, practical cooperation among major nations. The emphasis is on reforming the international order, not demolishing it,” he added.
Happymon Jacob, founder-director of the Council for Strategic and Defense Research, opined that “a strong BRICS would put India on the adversarial side of the U.S. and its allies, at a time when India’s most important relationships are with them.” Earlier this year, India concluded a free trade agreement with the European Union. And despite all its grievances, the U.S. is one of India’s top trading partners with bilateral trade worth an estimated $239.6 billion in 2025.
“BRICS is useful for hedging, and for keeping adversaries close, especially when friends are acting up. It is a messaging platform and a pressure group which brings leaders with very different views into the same room, where some of those differences get talked through, if not resolved,” he wrote in an opinion piece.
“BRICS, at best, is a pressure group. Its members are inside the U.S.-led order, despite their varying degrees of disagreements with it, and they use the grouping to put pressure on the U.S. for their individual gains –rhetoric in public and negotiations in private,” he added.
Perhaps the real achievement for India was that it was able to show its convening power; it managed to get high representatives from Iran, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia at one event and in the same room. Does that give India the credentials to become a possible mediator in future conflicts? Maybe, if India wants to. For now, the New Delhi BRICS Summit did provide a venue for the leaders of Iran and the UAE to sit down for a face-to-face conversation. That India managed a consensus New Delhi Declaration is also notable.
The BRICS also offered India a chance to re-align its position vis-à-vis Iran. At the start of the U.S.-Iran war, India was seen to be on the side of Israel, but New Delhi quietly corrected course subsequently, and the meeting between Modi and Iranian President Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek on August 31 was part of that strategy. Modi’s meeting with Pezeshkian in New Delhi on September 11 carried that conversation and course correction further. Interestingly, Pezeshkian was the only leader, among all those who visited, to call on Indian President Droupadi Murmu.
India’s focus on issues of importance to the Global South is in keeping with its efforts to position itself as its voice. BRICS being a diverse group, consensus on all issues will be hard to come by. The best that India can do is to steer the group away from big power rivalries, which it seems to have accomplished with the Delhi summit.

articles.title: Fighters Without Borders: Mercenaries, Adventurers, and Volunteers in Myanmar’s Civil War
articles.full_text:
The country’s civil wars have long attracted foreign nationals seeking adventure or driven by a mission. Are Russians the latest to join the fight?
Russian special forces soldiers take part in the opening ceremony of the “Tropical Storm” joint military exercise, the first-ever joint training maneuvers between the Russian and Myanmar militaries, in Naypyidaw, July 2026.
In July 2026, footage released by the Myanmar regime showed troops from Russia’s Airborne Forces, the Vozdushno-desantnye voyska Rossii (VDV), training alongside their Myanmar counterparts. The Myanmar–Russia joint exercise, named Tiger-2026, formed part of the expanding military cooperation between Naypyidaw and Moscow. The exercise was followed by a visit by the military-appointed President Min Aung Hlaing to Russia, during which the two sides signed a series of agreements and memoranda covering military and broader economic cooperation. In his meeting with President Putin, Min Aung Hlaing described Myanmar as a “reliable partner” of Russia.
Together, these developments show that the Kremlin is now an important partner for Min Aung Hlaing’s “civilian” government, despite his earlier overtures sometimes appearing to receive limited attention. The presence in Myanmar of VDV personnel, unmanned vehicles, and Russian military instructors has therefore prompted some observers to ask whether Moscow may become more deeply involved in Myanmar’s civil war in the months and years to come. But Moscow’s growing official military presence may not be the only way Russian nationals are becoming involved in Myanmar’s war. Recent evidence suggests that Russian “soldiers of fortune” may already be operating alongside Myanmar forces, raising the possibility of a more direct Russian presence on the battlefield.
The presence of foreign soldiers of fortune in Myanmar is hardly a new phenomenon. Indeed, it predates the founding of the modern nation itself. During the early years of the Second World War in Burma, a group of American airmen known as the American Volunteer Group, paid and equipped by the Chinese Nationalist government, briefly operated from airfields in British Burma. Popularly remembered as the Flying Tigers, these American pilots helped resist Japanese air raids over Rangoon. They were among the earliest foreign fighters to operate on this land. This is separate from the presence of the Chinese Expeditionary Force during the Burma Campaign, whose soldiers belonged to a national military and therefore cannot be categorized as mercenaries.
Under the post-independence government of U Nu, there were recurring, though often unconfirmed, reports of foreign military elements (i.e., Republican Chinese and American military advisors) connected to the remnants of Kuomintang forces that occupied parts of eastern Shan State after being driven out of China by Mao Zedong’s communist armies. The Kuomintang troops were supported through Air America, an airline covertly controlled by the United States Central Intelligence Agency. Its activities included delivering supplies to Kuomintang forces in Burma and supporting Hmong irregular forces during the “secret wars” in Laos and the wider Indochina conflict. The U Nu government formally protested these covert activities at the then newly established United Nations.
On the other side of the Cold War, revolutionary volunteers supported their ideological comrades. When the Communist Party of Burma established its Northeastern Military Region in 1968, its ranks included Chinese volunteers carrying copies of Mao’s “Little Red Book.” Some figures associated with the present-day leadership and origins of northeastern ethnic armed organizations, including the United Wa State Army, the National Democratic Alliance Army, and the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), either emerged from this Maoist revolutionary network or trace part of their political and military lineage to it.
At the other end of the country, the Karen National Union, under the leadership of General Saw Bo Mya, employed an assortment of foreign mercenaries, military contractors, and instructors in its expanding liberated areas throughout the 1980s. French mercenaries, in particular, arrived in Kawthoolei, the KNU-administered areas of southeastern Myanmar. Many were often former members of the French Foreign Legion who provided services as military instructors, advisers, and defensive planners. Commanders serving under Ne Win reportedly believed that these mercenaries contributed to the construction of the KNU’s network of major fortifications along the Thailand–Myanmar border. Myanmar military commanders also claimed to have captured letters and personal items belonging to these Frenchmen on the battlefield.
Even after major Myanmar military offensives in the 1990s brought down many of these fortifications, mercenaries and foreign volunteers continued to appear along the border. Throughout the late 1990s and 2000s, reports of foreign fighters in the region persisted. The networks and relationships created during the Cold War may have helped establish the borderlands as a potential destination for people offering military services.
During this period of military offensives, another kind of foreign participant entered Myanmar’s battlefields: the humanitarian volunteer. Following a series of missionary journeys to Myanmar’s war-ravaged borderlands and a meeting with Aung San Suu Kyi in 1996, former U.S. Special Forces officer David Eubank founded the Free Burma Rangers (FBR). Officially a humanitarian organization providing medical assistance and training, the group has worked closely with the KNU and other resistance organizations. It has transferred practical knowledge, provided training and, at times, participated in the armed protection of civilians. After the 2021 military coup, the FBR gained significantly greater visibility as large numbers of young people from Myanmar’s cities sought refuge in KNU-controlled territories. FBR helped to organize resistance forces and set up training programs for young urban evacuees.
The current international landscape has also seen an increase in foreign volunteers who are not primarily motivated by financial reward. One example is Azad and the Anti-Fascist Internationalist Front (AIF), a left-wing internationalist organization operating along the India–Myanmar border. Azad, a U.S. national and former participant in the Syrian Civil War, reportedly came to Myanmar because of an ideological commitment to fighting authoritarianism. Unlike many mercenaries from earlier periods, these internationalist volunteers appear to be motivated primarily by political conviction and solidarity. The AIF has claimed involvement in combat operations, including sniper and drone warfare, and has publicized a female-operated drone unit known as the Witch.
A series of arrests in India involving foreign nationals allegedly attempting to travel to Myanmar or support resistance organizations has offered further glimpses of this emerging international solidarity movement. Court filings from August 2026 by India’s National Investigation Agency alleged that these groups of Americans and Ukrainians were involved in training local resistance groups in drone assembly, operation, and logistics.
Khant, a People’s Defense Force trooper from southeastern Myanmar, has communicated to the authors that foreign nationals and diasporas who were sympathetic to the democratic resistance were key in fitting his company with tactical gear, night vision goggles, and other assorted equipment without the usual shades of war-profiteering and gun-running. The Australian national who was detained back in March 2026 by his own national authorities, after a trip from the Thailand-Myanmar border, was perhaps part of one of these supporter networks.
The available cases remain limited, but they show how Myanmar’s resistance has begun attracting not only members of the diaspora but also foreign volunteers motivated by anti-authoritarian politics or a personal identification with the struggle.
The post-coup conflict has also brought back another phenomenon from Myanmar’s earlier conflicts: the involvement of Chinese volunteers, veterans, and private security personnel. The MNDAA has long been reported to have recruited former members of China’s People’s Liberation Army (PLA). During its first attempt to retake Laukkai in 2015, reports emerged of Chinese nationals, former PLA members, fighting alongside the group. There is considerably less evidence of Chinese mercenaries participating directly in the Operation 1027 offensive, which the MNDAA and its partners launched in October 2023, and such claims must therefore be treated cautiously.
China’s broader role in Myanmar’s security landscape has nevertheless continued to expand. Even prior to the 2021 coup, China allowed a private security company, Frontier Security Group (FSG), to protect its jade mining interests in Northern Myanmar. The FSG had the Dark Prince, Eric Prince, former head of Blackwater, as a board member.
In the aftermath of Operation 1027, China and the Min Aung Hlaing regime agreed on establishing a joint security company, formally intended to protect Chinese investments and personnel. Chinese security interests are particularly concentrated around strategic infrastructure, including Kyaukphyu in Rakhine State, where major port, pipeline and economic corridor projects are located. Whether these security arrangements will remain limited to protecting Chinese projects or become entangled in Myanmar’s wider conflict remains an important question.
The latest and potentially most consequential addition to this diverse collection of foreign participants is the reported presence of Russian nationals on Myanmar’s battlefield. We have been examining possible Russian links to the conflict since at least 2023, initially asking whether the Wagner Group or similar Russian military networks might eventually establish a presence in the country. This concern emerged before the latest sightings and was rooted in both personal observations and the wider pattern of Russian activity abroad.
One of us first encountered Russian personnel in Meiktila in central Myanmar in 2016, three years after the communal violence that devastated the area. These personnel said that they were working with the Myanmar Air Force and showed videos of their activities, which included the training of pilots and officers and assisting with the repair of helicopters and other military equipment. This encounter did not establish any connection to Wagner. It did, however, demonstrate that Russian advisors had already developed an operational relationship with Myanmar’s military aviation and its personnel years before the 2021 coup.
Our earlier concerns were also influenced by a report published in May 2023 by the independent Russian outlet Verstka. The report examined a map visible behind Wagner founder Yevgeny Prigozhin during an interview with Russian political blogger Konstantin Dolgov. The map divided countries into different color-coded categories apparently related to Wagner’s international activities. Myanmar appeared in white, separate from countries where Wagner was understood to have personnel physically deployed. Although the meaning of this category was never conclusively established, it raised the possibility that Myanmar was being considered for, or was already receiving, some form of technical, strategic, or non-combat support.
At the time, there was no concrete evidence that Wagner personnel were operating inside Myanmar. We therefore treated the map and the earlier presence of Russian specialists as warning signs rather than proof. Nevertheless, they pointed towards a knowledge gap. While Wagner’s operations in Africa, the Middle East, and Ukraine have received extensive attention, far less is known about the group’s possible networks or ambitions in Southeast Asia. Myanmar’s deepening defence relationship with Russia made the possibility worthy of continued monitoring.
Our latest open-source investigation based on an anonymous tip has now identified a series of social-media posts apparently belonging to a Swedish-Estonian national, Viktor Azrael, with ties to Russian military networks and the now-defunct Wagner Group. This connection is based primarily on Azrael’s own account: in a 2023 social-media thread, he claimed that he had encountered Wagner personnel in Syria and later traveled to Russia intending to join the group. In posts from August 6, September 2, and September 5, 2025, he presents himself as conducting sniper training with Myanmar military personnel.
Later posts show him alongside a Russian national identified as Sasha. The material suggests that the two men may have operated in or traveled through a conflict area in southeastern Myanmar, possibly Karen State.
Some posts also claimed that the Russian fighters participated in sniper duels with American volunteers fighting on the resistance side. We have not independently verified this claim or established the identities and affiliations of the alleged American fighters.
What is nevertheless striking is how the journey was presented. Rather than describing himself as part of an official Russian deployment, the individual portrayed his time in Myanmar as an Asian adventure. This language points towards a long-standing but often overlooked category of foreign participant: the military adventurer motivated by a mixture of ideology, personal ambition, combat experience, and the love of the game itself.
The Wagner Group in its original form may no longer be the central question it was when these concerns were first raised. The more important issue is whether the networks, methods, and model associated with Wagner, which combine state interests, private military actors, technical specialists, and individuals whose official status remains deliberately unclear, could develop within the context of the growing Myanmar–Russia relationship.
Russian involvement in Myanmar may soon come to operate, if it does not already, at several levels: formal military cooperation between the two governments; the deployment of instructors and technical personnel; private or semi-private military networks; and individual Russian nationals traveling to the battlefield independently. If true, this simultaneous appearance raises legitimate questions about whether individual adventurers could eventually become part of a broader and more organized Russian presence.
Such a development would have consequences beyond Myanmar. A more permanent Russian military or private-security presence could alter the strategic environment of Southeast Asia and affect the security calculations of neighboring China and India. It would also deepen the international dimensions of a war that is still too often treated as an isolated domestic crisis.
Seen in this historical context, the recent reports that Russian snipers are present in Myanmar, in addition to the VDV personnel training with the Myanmar military, are less anomalous than they may initially seem. Foreigners have been participating in Myanmar’s wars for decades, although their motivations and affiliations have differed significantly. The conflict since 2021 has merely produced a new generation of foreign participants and created new routes through which they can become involved.
What remains uncertain is how far this latest wave will go. Will Russian snipers remain a handful of individual adventurers, or will they become part of a broader Russian military or private-security presence? The same questions apply to Chinese security personnel deployed to protect strategic infrastructure, and indeed to the volunteers fighting on the side of Myanmar’s resistance.
articles.summary: The country's civil wars have long attracted foreign nationals seeking adventure or driven by a mission. Are Russians the latest to join the fight?

articles.title: A Matter of Trust: Google, Artificial Intelligence, and the Public Sphere
articles.full_text:
Bertha Chan explains how Google seeks to mitigate risk while pushing forward the frontiers of AI.
Singapore-based Bertha Chan heads Trust and Safety Global Engagements across the Asia-Pacific for Google, focusing on the safeguards and considerations needed to prevent AI misuse while keeping pace with the technology.
Her remit covers jurisdictions and partnerships with governments and civil society, as well as combating the ever-evolving online scam industry, which is already adopting the latest advances in AI, especially the production of deepfakes.
Chan says that the foundation of all innovation and technology adoption has to be trust and that Google aims to protect its users at every part of their “entire digital journey,” adding that its email product, Gmail, stops 90 percent of spam, phishing and malware from ever reaching an inbox.
“So that’s what we call all safety by design,” Chan told The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt, adding that Google has deployed research teams that seek to establish policies and frameworks aimed at safeguarding children and families from dangerous and sexual content, and preventing fraud.
“These experts are advisors who specialize in a very wide range of expertise, for example, developmental psychology, cultural anthropology, human development, youth culture [and] youth behavior – when it comes to technology more,” Chan said.
“So with their expertise we collaborate and understand and seek to really fine-tune our products.”
Prior to Google, Chan drove digital transformation and international relations initiatives within the Singapore government. She holds a Master’s degree in sociology from the University of Oxford and a Bachelor’s degree in psychology from University College London.

articles.title: Cambodia, Thailand Begin Compulsory Conciliation in Maritime Boundary Dispute
articles.full_text:
The process, convened under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea, follows Thailand’s revocation of a 2001 MoU governing bilateral maritime talks.
Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn arrives at an UNCLOS conciliation meeting related to the Thailand-Cambodia maritime border dispute in Singapore, Sep. 15, 2026.
Cambodia and Thailand began compulsory conciliation proceedings in Singapore yesterday, aimed at resolving a long-running maritime dispute.
The three-day session marks the opening of a process conducted under Article 298 and Annex V of the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which is intended to resolve the two nations’ overlapping claims in the Gulf of Thailand.
After a closed-door session yesterday that was chaired by Katrina Cooper, the head of the Conciliation Commission, a public session took place today in which the Cambodian and Thai foreign ministers delivered opening statements laying out their governments’ respective positions.
Cambodian Foreign Minister Prak Sokhonn told the Commission that his government’s objective was “to achieve a resolution that serves the peoples of both nations and contributes to peace, cooperation and shared prosperity in the region.”
“A peaceful resolution is in the shared interests of both countries and will contribute to peace and stability in the region,” he said. “It will protect sovereignty, strengthen confidence, unlock energy resources, support development, and create new job opportunities not only for now, but also for the future generations of the Cambodian and Thai peoples.”
In his statement, Thailand’s Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkaew said that Thailand “enters this conciliation in good faith, fully mindful of the provisions of UNCLOS.” He added that his government “stands ready to engage in this process constructively, with the aim of achieving, with the Commission’s assistance, a negotiated and equitable solution.”
The maritime dispute ‌between Cambodia and Thailand relates to a 26,000-square-kilometer area in the Gulf of Thailand, known as the Overlapping Claims Area (OCA). The OCA is estimated to hold abundant reserves of oil and natural gas, the exploitation of which has become more pressing due to the current global oil supply crisis.
Maritime tensions between Phnom Penh and Bangkok have increased in parallel with the intensification of the dispute over the Thailand-Cambodia land border, which flared into conflict twice last year – for five days in July and then for nearly three weeks in December – killing nearly 150 people and displacing around a million on both sides of the border.
Cambodia initiated the UNCLOS process in June, shortly after Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul’s government unilaterally cancelled a 2001 agreement with Cambodia that governed joint offshore energy exploration and the demarcation of maritime boundaries in the OCA. Anutin denied that the cancelation had anything to do with the tensions over the land border, instead citing the lack of progress made under the agreement.
In his statement yesterday, Prak Sokhonn said that after the cancelation of the MoU, Cambodia chose to initiate compulsory conciliation in order to “find a peaceful pathway forward in accordance with international law.” He added that Phnom Penh “sees this conciliation process as a means to rebuild trust, not as a form of escalation.”
⁠Sihasak was in general more combative, accusing Cambodia of taking refuge behind international law, while “repeatedly vilif[ying] Thailand through false narratives, distortion of facts, and unfounded accusations.” He added that Thailand had chosen to cancel the 2001 MoU because it “had produced no concrete progress” and that the government “chose to give negotiations a fresh start.” Sihasak also claimed that Thailand had offered direct bilateral talks over the maritime boundary, and expressed disappointment that Cambodia chose to initiate compulsory conciliation. “Thailand has consistently believed that differences between neighbors should be addressed through dialogue,” he said.
The Thai foreign minister also stated that the conciliation proceedings concerned “only maritime boundary delimitation between Thailand and Cambodia in the Gulf of Thailand” and would not address the island of Koh Kut, part of which was claimed by Cambodia in a continental shelf claim submitted in 1972.
Thai nationalist fears over Koh Kut derailed attempts by a previous Thai government to negotiate with Cambodia a resolution of the OCA in late 2024 and early 2025. This created tensions that quickly snowballed into armed clashes on the land border. The potential loss of Koh Kut is also why Thai nationalist lobby groups have long pushed for the cancellation of the 2001 MoU.
According to Annex V of UNCLOS, compulsory conciliation is a process in which a panel of independent experts – known as conciliators – examines a dispute and helps states parties reach an amicable settlement. Its findings are not legally binding on either party, but the process offers a way of discussing complex and sensitive disputes away from the domestic political hothouse.
The mechanism has only ever been invoked once before, in 2016, when Timor-Leste opted to refer its maritime dispute with Australia to compulsory conciliation. In that instance, Australia accepted conciliation and the five conciliators were able to offer a compromise that was ultimately accepted by both parties.
It is too soon to determine whether the UNCLOS process will allow Cambodia and Thailand to reach a similarly felicitous arrangement. The maritime dispute stems from divergent interpretations of a land border treaty signed between Siam and French Indochina in 1907. This did not delineate the maritime border but provided a point on land from which both countries have charted their claims.
In principle, the maritime dispute should be a lot easier to resolve than the disagreements over the land border. The latter involves more intricate questions of demarcation undertaken by French colonial cartographers, as well as the presence of Angkorian temple ruins that are charged with cultural and political significance, particularly for the Cambodian side.
However, as the tone of Sihasak’s address suggests, last year’s armed clashes have poisoned relations between Bangkok and Phnom Penh to such an extent that any agreement between the two sides, even one that opens the way to mutual exploitation of rich undersea resources, will be challenging.
The UNCLOS process probably offers the best means of reaching a resolution, but any recommendations handed down by the Conciliation Commission will still need to be “sold” to publics that are touchy about sovereignty and liable to pounce at the merest hint of compromise. This is particularly the case in Thailand. Indeed, Thai nationalist agitation is the primary reason that the two nations made so little progress in negotiating maritime border issues under the 2001 MoU.

articles.title: Why Some of Southeast Asia’s Digital Banks are Starting to Scale
articles.full_text:
Can these institutions threaten the entrenched conventional mega-banks that dominate the region’s financial landscape?
An online advertisement for MariBank, a digital bank based in Singapore.
The world of digital banking is an odd place. A digital bank offers the same basic services as a traditional bank – takes deposits, makes loans – but it does it almost entirely online, eliminating much of the overhead required to maintain a network of brick and mortar branches. Digital banks in this context are standalone businesses, as opposed to digital offshoots of existing banks like Jenius in Indonesia or Trust Bank in Singapore. In fact, if the business model can scale, digital banks might pose a serious threat to the entrenched position of conventional mega-banks that dominate Southeast Asia’s financial landscape.
Despite the promise, digital banking has developed unevenly across Southeast Asia. In Vietnam, there are no true digital banks as digital finance platforms must partner with or be a subsidiary of an existing commercial bank. Regulators in Thailand have also moved slowly in getting the first few digital banks up and running and big potential players, like CP Group’s Ascend Bank, have encountered delays.  Indonesia sits on the other end of the spectrum, with digital banks backed by major tech and telecom firms seeing take-off, adding billions in customer deposits and rapidly scaling their loan portfolios over the last few years.
Indonesia’s experience provides some clues about when, why and how digital banks can scale. A key consideration is the regulatory environment. A regulatory system that is supportive of digital banks can open the door for new entrants to challenge incumbents and introduce potentially disruptive innovation into existing systems of banking and finance. Indonesian regulators showed an early willingness to allow this, which is not that surprising given there was a larger tech sector boom underway at the time. That boom has deflated somewhat now, although digital banks remain one of the more promising and profitable legacies of the boom.
In countries with more mature banking sectors, like Singapore, regulators have been cautious in growing digital banks, despite approving the first round of full licenses several years ago. MariBank, owned by tech conglomerate Sea, launched in 2022. Because MariBank is integrated into the Sea ecosystem, which includes its enormous e-commerce arm Shopee, it had amassed S$1.9 billion in deposits by 2025. But limited by tight regulatory oversight, MariBank made only S$222 million in loans and posted a S$56 million loss.
GSX bank, a partnership between telecom giant Singtel and online ride-hailing company Grab, tells a similar story with S$1.8 billion in deposits against S$777 million in loans, and a net loss in 2025. In both cases, the majority of their assets are parked with the central bank or in government and corporate bonds. GSX’s Malaysian arm, GX Bank Berhad, has also been slow out of the gate, reporting total assets of $479 million as of 2025 and a loan to deposit ratio of just 25 percent. There are signs, however, that activity may finally be picking up, with loans jumping 76 percent between December 2025 and June 2026.
In addition to permissive regulatory conditions, the scalability of digital banks depends to a large extent on who is backing them and how digital banking services can be integrated into wider existing commercial ecosystems. In particular, companies that have existing customer networks and use big digital platforms, like telecom and e-commerce companies, have an advantage.
In the Philippines, digital banking appears to be down to a two-horse race between Sea (a familiar refrain by now) and local telecom major PLDT. By the end of 2025, Sea’s MariBank Philippines had assets of just over $1 billion, with its loan portfolio growing 64 percent year over year. Maya Bank, in which PLDT is the main shareholder, reported $1.25 billion in assets and saw its loan book jump 86 percent compared to 2024.
This aligns with what we are seeing in Indonesia, where a friendly regulatory environment combined with backing from major tech, telecom and institutional investors has been decisive in determining which digital banks are scaling and which are stagnating. A very similar story is playing out in the Philippines, while in other countries, even if the institutional backing is there, the regulatory environment may be moving more slowly. For the time being, that’s what is holding back the kind of explosive growth one might have expected when regulators first started issuing digital banking licenses several years ago.
